harder.updated_question: Global prospect of reducing dependence on oil and gas: Environmental necessity for a sustainable future
harder.verification_criterion: The answer discusses specific strategies, technologies, or pathways for reducing global dependence on fossil fuels (oil and gas) in the context of environmental sustainability, such as renewable energy adoption, electrification, energy efficiency improvements, or policy frameworks.

attempts.answer:
# Executive Summary

<cite id="b98d63d1-0">Global warming is currently on track to exceed 2.7°C under existing policies, underscoring that deep reductions in oil and gas dependence are an environmental necessity to stay near 1.5–2°C targets</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-0">Net‑zero pathways cut global energy use by about a seventh by 2050, more than double clean energy investments to roughly $5 trillion per year by 2030, and reduce fossil fuels to about one‑fifth of total energy supply, requiring 4% annual energy intensity gains through 2030</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-2">Integrated assessment ensembles and IEA analysis converge that rapid electrification, step‑change energy efficiency, and scaling of renewables are central, with 70–85% renewable electricity by 2050 and near‑zero shares of coal and very low gas shares in typical 1.5°C pathways</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-0">A full phase‑out of fossil fuels by 2050 is technically feasible but demands 1.6–1.8× power generation growth relative to cost‑effective 1.5°C pathways, accelerated solar/wind and electrolyser deployment, and up to 34% higher lifetime energy supply investments</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-1">Realizing these transitions will require major emissions cuts in hard‑to‑abate transport and industry, with oil products and gas persisting mainly via electricity and fuels until deep electrification and low‑carbon alternatives scale</cite>.

# Why Reducing Oil and Gas Dependence Is Environmentally Necessary

<cite id="e2059a53-4">Limiting warming to 1.5°C requires global CO2 emissions to fall by about 45% from 2010 levels by 2030 and reach net zero around 2050</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-0">If current policies prevail, warming approaches 2.7°C (50% probability), while current pledges bring about 2.1°C, indicating that without rapid fossil fuel phase‑downs and electrification, climate targets are out of reach</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-3">The first Global Stocktake at COP28 emphasized urgent action to transition away from fossil fuels across energy systems for all warming‑limit scenarios</cite>. <cite id="4445961f-4">Consistent IEA pathways to meet 2°C rely on deep decarbonization of power and fuels, with fossil shares falling and renewables rising to meet electricity and transport needs, illustrating that sustained oil and gas reliance locks in overshoot risk</cite>.

# What a Global Reduction Pathway Looks Like

<cite id="b98d63d1-0">Net‑zero energy systems by 2050 imply shrinking fossil fuels to one‑fifth of energy supply from four‑fifths today, with global energy demand falling by 8% even as population and economies grow</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-1">Across Paris‑aligned scenarios, decarbonization replaces fossil use primarily through direct electrification powered by renewables, with remaining hard‑to‑abate emissions addressed by CCS and carbon dioxide removal</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-2">Typical 1.5°C pathways accelerate electrification, cut final energy use through efficiency, raise the share of low‑emission electricity to 70–85% by 2050, and drive gas‑power shares toward near‑zero alongside very low coal shares</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-2">Transport electrification and biofuel shares rise modestly by 2040 in some scenarios, while overall fossil shares remain dominant absent stronger policy and investment shifts, highlighting sectoral lags</cite>. <cite id="4445961f-1">Electricity demand rises across scenarios, with renewables dominating by 70–90% of generation by 2050 and fossil shares declining, reinforcing the centrality of clean power to de‑carbonizing fuels and mobility</cite>.

# Hard-to-Abate Sectors and Alternatives

<cite id="b98d63d1-2">Industry and buildings require 95% emissions cuts by 2050, implying deep retrofits and process changes, with transport still heavily reliant on fossil fuels unless electrification and alternative fuels rapidly scale</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-3">Hydrogen can complement electricity in hard‑to‑electrify segments; in a net‑zero‑aligned case, hydrogen rises to ~5% of energy demand by 2040 from electrolysers, with full green supply maturity by 2060 as renewables and nuclear scale</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-0">Achieving net zero with a full fossil phase‑out increases the need for electrolysers and 1.6–1.8× power generation relative to cost‑effective pathways, underscoring the role of power system flexibility and storage</cite>. <cite id="4445961f-2">Across multi‑model analyses for Japan, total electricity increases toward net zero while fossil shares fall, with BECCS and traded synthetic carriers supplementing the mix, though oil remains present in some sectors</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-1">Biofuels and electrified public transport can reduce road emissions, but air and maritime transport remain fossil‑heavy absent rapid electrification or sustainable aviation/marine fuels at scale</cite>.

# Near-Term Milestones and Time Scales

<cite id="e2059a53-4">Halving cumulative 2010‑level CO2 emissions by 2030 is a central near‑term milestone for limiting warming to 1.5°C, with net zero around 2050</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-0">To meet net‑zero energy trajectories, energy intensity must improve by 4% per year through 2030 (roughly triple the pace of the past two decades) even as the global economy grows</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-1">By 2040, electricity demand is projected to rise by about 80% to roughly 39,000 TWh in IEA scenarios, with renewables rising from 21% in 2012 to 33% by 2040</cite>. <cite id="4445961f-4">Even 2°C‑consistent IEA pathways require a lower 2030 fossil share (e.g., 58% of electricity mix) and lower total energy demand than business‑as‑usual, indicating that 2030 is a decisive inflection point</cite>. <cite id="4445961f-2">In net‑zero scenarios, coal declines sharply by 2030 in most models, with phase‑out timing ranging from 2030 to after 2050, and gas falling as renewables scale</cite>.

# Investment Implications and Economic Transformation

<cite id="b98d63d1-0">Global energy investments must more than double to about $5 trillion per year by 2030, with positive GDP effects, while fossil fuel use shrinks and efficiency, renewables, and innovation dominate</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-0">Phase‑out pathways can increase lifetime energy supply investments by up to 34% but reduce reliance on costly carbon dioxide removal, improving climate risk resilience</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-3">Case studies show that accelerating renewable and nuclear buildout, coupled with electrification and green hydrogen, can deliver 90% system‑wide emissions reductions by 2040, though industrial emitters face significant decarbonization challenges</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-1">Without rapid shifts, oil and gas remain dominant in mobility and heating, locking in higher long‑run emissions and stranded asset risks as low‑carbon alternatives diffuse</cite>.

# Risks, Governance, and Energy Security

<cite id="b98d63d1-0">Meeting net zero requires retiring fossil plants and retooling infrastructure, implying risks of stranded assets and financing shifts if transition policies are insufficient</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-1">Policy momentum toward fossil phase‑out has grown post‑COP28, with G7 commitment to phase out existing unabated coal by the 2030s and broader recognition that rapid electrification and renewables are core to Paris goals</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-2">Sectoral analyses indicate uneven progress: road transport shows partial electrification, while aviation and shipping remain fossil‑dependent, necessitating coordinated standards, fueling infrastructure, and international cooperation</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-1">Geopolitical and market volatility in oil/gas can undermine energy security and emissions targets unless diversified with large‑scale renewables, storage, and grid interconnections</cite>. <cite id="4445961f-1">Rising electricity demand through 2050 requires planning for variable renewable integration, grid reinforcements, and hydrogen or imports to manage sectoral decarbonization</cite>.

# Environmental Limits and Carbon Budget Consistency

<cite id="b98d63d1-4">IEA’s Blue Map 2050 corresponds to limiting CO2 to 450 ppm in 2050, requiring a 50% cut from 2005 levels (77% relative to a 2050 baseline), with bioenergy, electricity, and fuels shifting to meet transport and energy needs</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-0">Meeting net‑zero energy outcomes demands that fossil fuels fall to about one‑fifth of energy supply by 2050 and that final energy demand in industry, transport, and buildings drop by 95% relative to business‑as‑usual, consistent with cumulative carbon budget constraints</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-3">Urgent and sustained fossil fuel reductions are necessary to avoid overshoot scenarios that would require unprecedented and unproven CO2 removal at scale</cite>.

# Practical Pathways Forward

- Power and industry: <cite id="e2059a53-2">Scale variable renewable electricity to 70–85% of generation by 2050, pair with electrification of end‑uses and near‑zero coal/gas power</cite>. <cite id="4445961f-2">Use BECCS and synthetic carriers for residual emissions where feasible, recognizing sector‑specific constraints</cite>.
- Transport: <cite id="b98d63d1-1">Accelerate EV deployment and charging, develop sustainable aviation and maritime fuels, and expand electrified rail</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-0">Increase EV adoption and public transport electrification to bend the emissions curve faster than under current policies</cite>.
- Buildings and industry: <cite id="b98d63d1-0">Drive energy efficiency and retrofits to meet 4% per‑year energy intensity gains, complemented by process electrification and hydrogen for hard‑to‑abate uses</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-3">Deploy district heating electrification and hydrogen blends where grid quality allows, and expand low‑carbon industrial feedstocks</cite>.
- Finance and governance: <cite id="b98d63d1-0">Double annual energy investments to $5T by 2030 and reallocate capital from stranded fossil assets toward renewables, storage, and grid</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-0">Align carbon pricing and fossil leasing rules with net‑zero trajectories, and incentivize electrolysers and flexible power to meet 1.6–1.8× generation needs in phase‑out pathways</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-1">Coordinate international standards and public‑private investment to accelerate deployment in hard‑to‑abate sectors</cite>.

# Outlook and Remaining Gaps

<cite id="b98d63d1-2">If current fossil‑heavy trajectories persist, warming will exceed 2°C by mid‑century, with transport and industry emissions remaining high unless electrification and alternatives accelerate</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-0">A full fossil phase‑out by 2050 is technically feasible with accelerated electrification, renewables, and electrolysers, but at higher upfront investment, underscoring the need for decisive near‑term policy</cite>. <cite id="4445961f-2">Regional models show net‑zero systems increasingly dominated by renewables and lower oil/gas shares by 2050, though oil persists in some final uses, highlighting the importance of end‑use innovation and trade</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-1">Key uncertainties include methane leakage from remaining gas systems, uneven sectoral adoption, and the pace of innovation in aviation/sea fuels</cite>. Closing these gaps requires transparent, methane‑constrained fossil policies, rapid EV uptake, and accelerated deployment of hydrogen and bioeconomy solutions tailored to hard‑to‑abate sectors.

# Bottom Line

<cite id="b98d63d1-0">Reducing dependence on oil and gas is the central pillar of a sustainable energy system: it halves fossil shares of energy, cuts power’s carbon intensity to near zero, and redirects trillions in investment toward clean, efficient, and electrified systems</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-2">These shifts are consistent with 1.5–2°C limits only if they begin now at scale</cite>, with 2030 a pivotal inflection point for locking in long‑run climate outcomes. <cite id="e2059a53-0">Orderly phase‑out pathways increase upfront costs but avoid deeper reliance on unproven CO2 removal and systemic shocks, making them the environmentally necessary foundation for a sustainable future</cite>.

Title: Challenges and opportunities of the full phase-out of fossil fuels under the 1.5 °C goal
Snippet: The COP28 decision called for transitioning away from fossil fuels, sparking a growing interest in their full phase-out. However, energy system transformation pathways towards a phase-out of fossil fuels, which may reduce the reliance on carbon dioxide removal to meet the 1.5 °C goal, remain unclear. Here, we employ two global energy system models to explore energy system transformations and the challenges and opportunities associated with attaining a full phase-out of fossil fuels. We found that phasing out fossil fuels by 2050 would require accelerating direct and indirect electrification, involving 1.6–1.8-fold increases in power generation compared to the conventional cost-effective 1.5 °C pathways. This transition from cost-effective to fossil fuel phase-out pathways would increase energy supply investments by up to 34% over this century and require accelerated deployment of solar and wind power, as well as electrolysers. Despite opportunities including lower reliance on carbon dioxide removal and increasing probability of returning to 1.5 °C after temperature overshoot, these additional requirements imply that international society must approach the transition towards zero-fossil energy systems with strong determination. There is a lack of energy system transformation pathways required to achieve a full phase-out of fossil fuels by 2050 in the literature. This paper finds it requires rapid electrification and 1.6–1.8-fold increases in power generation compared to cost-effective 1.5 °C pathways.
</snippet>
<snippet id=e2059a53-1>
Title: Challenges and opportunities of the full phase-out of fossil fuels under the 1.5 °C goal
Snippet: Although the final decision does not explicitly mention a full phase-out, momentum is growing for the phase-out of fossil fuels to become a key focus of climate policies moving forward from COP28. Notably, in 2024, the Group of Seven (G7) committed to phasing out existing unabated coal power generation during the first half of the 2030s 4 , and the Group of Twenty (G20) leaders fully subscribed to the outcome of COP28, in particular the UAE Consensus and the GST-1 5 . 

The decarbonisation and defossilisation of energy systems could follow different energy transformation pathways. These differences may concern the pace, sequence, and stringency of fossil fuel phase-out, especially in sectors that are technically and economically challenging to decarbonise. Scenarios from integrated assessment models (IAMs) and energy system models have provided insights into energy transformation pathways in line with the long-term goals of the Paris Agreement [6][7][8][9][10][11][12] , as reflected in assessment reports by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), e.g., the Sixth Assessment Report (IPCC AR6) 13 . To obtain robust insights from previous studies, thousands of scenarios were submitted to the IPCC AR6 scenario database for analysis by IPCC Working Group III 14 . These scenario ensembles suggested that costeffective decarbonisation pathways involve replacing fossil fuel consumption primarily through direct electrification with renewable electricity, while also addressing CO 2 emissions from hard-toabate fossil fuel consumption through incorporating carbon capture and storage (CCS) and offsetting via carbon dioxide removal (CDR) 15 . 

However, achieving what could be called a zero-fossil (ZF) energy system, beyond transitioning away from and phasing out fossil fuels, will likely require pathways that depart from these typical decarbonisation pathways. Such differences are likely to arise because ZF energy systems require the elimination of even hard-to-abate fossil fuel consumption, which would remain in a typical 1.5 °C energy system [16][17][18][19] .
</snippet>
<snippet id=e2059a53-2>
Title: Integration of energy systems
Snippet: The United Nation's dedicated body for assessing climate change, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), released the report "Global Warming of 1.5°C" to identify the risks and offer mitigation options in the face of a rapidly warming world. 6 With the exception of "overshoot" scenarios as described by the IPCC, 2050 is the definitive year in which net-zero levels of global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions must be met. Achieving net zero by 2050 implies all fossil fuel consumption needs to be replaced with or converted to zero-carbon energy alternatives. If GHG emissions continued past 2050, as in the overshoot scenarios, billions of tons of carbon dioxide would need to be removed from the atmosphere annually, using technology that has not yet been applied on a global scale.

Title: Challenges and opportunities of the full phase-out of fossil fuels under the 1.5 °C goal
Snippet: The COP28 decision called for transitioning away from fossil fuels, sparking a growing interest in their full phase-out. However, energy system transformation pathways towards a phase-out of fossil fuels, which may reduce the reliance on carbon dioxide removal to meet the 1.5 °C goal, remain unclear. Here, we employ two global energy system models to explore energy system transformations and the challenges and opportunities associated with attaining a full phase-out of fossil fuels. We found that phasing out fossil fuels by 2050 would require accelerating direct and indirect electrification, involving 1.6-1.8-fold increases in power generation compared to the conventional costeffective 1.5 °C pathways. This transition from cost-effective to fossil fuel phase-out pathways would increase energy supply investments by up to 34% over this century and require accelerated deployment of solar and wind power, as well as electrolysers. Despite opportunities including lower reliance on carbon dioxide removal and increasing probability of returning to 1.5 °C after temperature overshoot, these additional requirements imply that international society must approach the transition towards zero-fossil energy systems with strong determination. 

Limiting global warming to well below 2 °C, and pursuing efforts to return to 1.5 °C after temporary overshoot by the end of the century in line with the Paris Agreement, requires a rapid reduction of fossil fuel contributions to the energy system 1,2 . The final decision of the first Global Stocktake (GST-1) at the 2023 United Nations Conference of the Parties (COP28) highlighted the necessity for urgent action to address the climate crisis, given that the Parties are not on track to achieve the long-term goals of the Paris Agreement 3 . A key achievement of the GST-1 decision was that it called for all Parties to contribute to global efforts, particularly transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems. Although the final decision does not explicitly mention a full phase-out, momentum is growing for the phase-out of fossil fuels to become a key focus of climate policies moving forward from COP28.

# Executive Summary

<cite id="b98d63d1-0">Global warming is currently on track to exceed 2.7°C under existing policies, underscoring that deep reductions in oil and gas dependence are an environmental necessity to stay near 1.5–2°C targets</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-0">Net‑zero pathways cut global energy use by about a seventh by 2050, more than double clean energy investments to roughly $5 trillion per year by 2030, and reduce fossil fuels to about one‑fifth of total energy supply, requiring 4% annual energy intensity gains through 2030</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-2">Integrated assessment ensembles and IEA analysis converge that rapid electrification, step‑change energy efficiency, and scaling of renewables are central, with 70–85% renewable electricity by 2050 and near‑zero shares of coal and very low gas shares in typical 1.5°C pathways</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-0">A full phase‑out of fossil fuels by 2050 is technically feasible but demands 1.6–1.8× power generation growth relative to cost‑effective 1.5°C pathways, accelerated solar/wind and electrolyser deployment, and up to 34% higher lifetime energy supply investments</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-1">Realizing these transitions will require major emissions cuts in hard‑to‑abate transport and industry, with oil products and gas persisting mainly via electricity and fuels until deep electrification and low‑carbon alternatives scale</cite>.

# Why Reducing Oil and Gas Dependence Is Environmentally Necessary

<cite id="e2059a53-4">Limiting warming to 1.5°C requires global CO2 emissions to fall by about 45% from 2010 levels by 2030 and reach net zero around 2050</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-0">If current policies prevail, warming approaches 2.7°C (50% probability), while current pledges bring about 2.1°C, indicating that without rapid fossil fuel phase‑downs and electrification, climate targets are out of reach</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-3">The first Global Stocktake at COP28 emphasized urgent action to transition away from fossil fuels across energy systems for all warming‑limit scenarios</cite>. <cite id="4445961f-4">Consistent IEA pathways to meet 2°C rely on deep decarbonization of power and fuels, with fossil shares falling and renewables rising to meet electricity and transport needs, illustrating that sustained oil and gas reliance locks in overshoot risk</cite>.

# What a Global Reduction Pathway Looks Like

<cite id="b98d63d1-0">Net‑zero energy systems by 2050 imply shrinking fossil fuels to one‑fifth of energy supply from four‑fifths today, with global energy demand falling by 8% even as population and economies grow</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-1">Across Paris‑aligned scenarios, decarbonization replaces fossil use primarily through direct electrification powered by renewables, with remaining hard‑to‑abate emissions addressed by CCS and carbon dioxide removal</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-2">Typical 1.5°C pathways accelerate electrification, cut final energy use through efficiency, raise the share of low‑emission electricity to 70–85% by 2050, and drive gas‑power shares toward near‑zero alongside very low coal shares</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-2">Transport electrification and biofuel shares rise modestly by 2040 in some scenarios, while overall fossil shares remain dominant absent stronger policy and investment shifts, highlighting sectoral lags</cite>. <cite id="4445961f-1">Electricity demand rises across scenarios, with renewables dominating by 70–90% of generation by 2050 and fossil shares declining, reinforcing the centrality of clean power to de‑carbonizing fuels and mobility</cite>.

# Hard-to-Abate Sectors and Alternatives

<cite id="b98d63d1-2">Industry and buildings require 95% emissions cuts by 2050, implying deep retrofits and process changes, with transport still heavily reliant on fossil fuels unless electrification and alternative fuels rapidly scale</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-3">Hydrogen can complement electricity in hard‑to‑electrify segments; in a net‑zero‑aligned case, hydrogen rises to ~5% of energy demand by 2040 from electrolysers, with full green supply maturity by 2060 as renewables and nuclear scale</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-0">Achieving net zero with a full fossil phase‑out increases the need for electrolysers and 1.6–1.8× power generation relative to cost‑effective pathways, underscoring the role of power system flexibility and storage</cite>. <cite id="4445961f-2">Across multi‑model analyses for Japan, total electricity increases toward net zero while fossil shares fall, with BECCS and traded synthetic carriers supplementing the mix, though oil remains present in some sectors</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-1">Biofuels and electrified public transport can reduce road emissions, but air and maritime transport remain fossil‑heavy absent rapid electrification or sustainable aviation/marine fuels at scale</cite>.

# Near-Term Milestones and Time Scales

<cite id="e2059a53-4">Halving cumulative 2010‑level CO2 emissions by 2030 is a central near‑term milestone for limiting warming to 1.5°C, with net zero around 2050</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-0">To meet net‑zero energy trajectories, energy intensity must improve by 4% per year through 2030 (roughly triple the pace of the past two decades) even as the global economy grows</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-1">By 2040, electricity demand is projected to rise by about 80% to roughly 39,000 TWh in IEA scenarios, with renewables rising from 21% in 2012 to 33% by 2040</cite>. <cite id="4445961f-4">Even 2°C‑consistent IEA pathways require a lower 2030 fossil share (e.g., 58% of electricity mix) and lower total energy demand than business‑as‑usual, indicating that 2030 is a decisive inflection point</cite>. <cite id="4445961f-2">In net‑zero scenarios, coal declines sharply by 2030 in most models, with phase‑out timing ranging from 2030 to after 2050, and gas falling as renewables scale</cite>.

# Investment Implications and Economic Transformation

<cite id="b98d63d1-0">Global energy investments must more than double to about $5 trillion per year by 2030, with positive GDP effects, while fossil fuel use shrinks and efficiency, renewables, and innovation dominate</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-0">Phase‑out pathways can increase lifetime energy supply investments by up to 34% but reduce reliance on costly carbon dioxide removal, improving climate risk resilience</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-3">Case studies show that accelerating renewable and nuclear buildout, coupled with electrification and green hydrogen, can deliver 90% system‑wide emissions reductions by 2040, though industrial emitters face significant decarbonization challenges</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-1">Without rapid shifts, oil and gas remain dominant in mobility and heating, locking in higher long‑run emissions and stranded asset risks as low‑carbon alternatives diffuse</cite>.

# Risks, Governance, and Energy Security

<cite id="b98d63d1-0">Meeting net zero requires retiring fossil plants and retooling infrastructure, implying risks of stranded assets and financing shifts if transition policies are insufficient</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-1">Policy momentum toward fossil phase‑out has grown post‑COP28, with G7 commitment to phase out existing unabated coal by the 2030s and broader recognition that rapid electrification and renewables are core to Paris goals</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-2">Sectoral analyses indicate uneven progress: road transport shows partial electrification, while aviation and shipping remain fossil‑dependent, necessitating coordinated standards, fueling infrastructure, and international cooperation</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-1">Geopolitical and market volatility in oil/gas can undermine energy security and emissions targets unless diversified with large‑scale renewables, storage, and grid interconnections</cite>. <cite id="4445961f-1">Rising electricity demand through 2050 requires planning for variable renewable integration, grid reinforcements, and hydrogen or imports to manage sectoral decarbonization</cite>.

# Environmental Limits and Carbon Budget Consistency

<cite id="b98d63d1-4">IEA’s Blue Map 2050 corresponds to limiting CO2 to 450 ppm in 2050, requiring a 50% cut from 2005 levels (77% relative to a 2050 baseline), with bioenergy, electricity, and fuels shifting to meet transport and energy needs</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-0">Meeting net‑zero energy outcomes demands that fossil fuels fall to about one‑fifth of energy supply by 2050 and that final energy demand in industry, transport, and buildings drop by 95% relative to business‑as‑usual, consistent with cumulative carbon budget constraints</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-3">Urgent and sustained fossil fuel reductions are necessary to avoid overshoot scenarios that would require unprecedented and unproven CO2 removal at scale</cite>.

# Practical Pathways Forward

- Power and industry: <cite id="e2059a53-2">Scale variable renewable electricity to 70–85% of generation by 2050, pair with electrification of end‑uses and near‑zero coal/gas power</cite>. <cite id="4445961f-2">Use BECCS and synthetic carriers for residual emissions where feasible, recognizing sector‑specific constraints</cite>.
- Transport: <cite id="b98d63d1-1">Accelerate EV deployment and charging, develop sustainable aviation and maritime fuels, and expand electrified rail</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-0">Increase EV adoption and public transport electrification to bend the emissions curve faster than under current policies</cite>.
- Buildings and industry: <cite id="b98d63d1-0">Drive energy efficiency and retrofits to meet 4% per‑year energy intensity gains, complemented by process electrification and hydrogen for hard‑to‑abate uses</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-3">Deploy district heating electrification and hydrogen blends where grid quality allows, and expand low‑carbon industrial feedstocks</cite>.
- Finance and governance: <cite id="b98d63d1-0">Double annual energy investments to $5T by 2030 and reallocate capital from stranded fossil assets toward renewables, storage, and grid</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-0">Align carbon pricing and fossil leasing rules with net‑zero trajectories, and incentivize electrolysers and flexible power to meet 1.6–1.8× generation needs in phase‑out pathways</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-1">Coordinate international standards and public‑private investment to accelerate deployment in hard‑to‑abate sectors</cite>.

# Outlook and Remaining Gaps

<cite id="b98d63d1-2">If current fossil‑heavy trajectories persist, warming will exceed 2°C by mid‑century, with transport and industry emissions remaining high unless electrification and alternatives accelerate</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-0">A full fossil phase‑out by 2050 is technically feasible with accelerated electrification, renewables, and electrolysers, but at higher upfront investment, underscoring the need for decisive near‑term policy</cite>. <cite id="4445961f-2">Regional models show net‑zero systems increasingly dominated by renewables and lower oil/gas shares by 2050, though oil persists in some final uses, highlighting the importance of end‑use innovation and trade</cite>. <cite id="b98d63d1-1">Key uncertainties include methane leakage from remaining gas systems, uneven sectoral adoption, and the pace of innovation in aviation/sea fuels</cite>. Closing these gaps requires transparent, methane‑constrained fossil policies, rapid EV uptake, and accelerated deployment of hydrogen and bioeconomy solutions tailored to hard‑to‑abate sectors.

# Bottom Line

<cite id="b98d63d1-0">Reducing dependence on oil and gas is the central pillar of a sustainable energy system: it halves fossil shares of energy, cuts power’s carbon intensity to near zero, and redirects trillions in investment toward clean, efficient, and electrified systems</cite>. <cite id="e2059a53-2">These shifts are consistent with 1.5–2°C limits only if they begin now at scale</cite>, with 2030 a pivotal inflection point for locking in long‑run climate outcomes. <cite id="e2059a53-0">Orderly phase‑out pathways increase upfront costs but avoid deeper reliance on unproven CO2 removal and systemic shocks, making them the environmentally necessary foundation for a sustainable future</cite>.
</answer>

Title: The Role of Trade in Asia and the Pacific’s Net Zero Pathways: Overview and Policy Implications
Snippet: The International Energy Agency (IEA 2021) conducted a comprehensive study on the net zero transition for the energy sector, which accounts for three-fourths of greenhouse gases. The influential study put forward three main scenarios: (i) Stated Policy Scenario, including specific plans already in place or announced by governments; (ii) Announcement Pledges Case, where all announced national zero pledges were assumed to be achieved on time; and (iii) Net Zero Scenario by 2050, which forms the core of the analysis in the paper. The Stated Policy Scenario would lead global temperatures to rise 2.7°C, while the rise in the Pledges Case scenarios would be 2.1°C (each with a 50% probability). Net zero would be consistent with a 1.5°C rise (with a 50% probability). 

The study's net zero scenario stipulates the necessary conditions for the global energy sector to reach net zero emissions by 2050. 17 The policy challenges are daunting. The net zero pathway assumes the world economy in 2030 will be two-fifths larger than today but will use 7% less energy, requiring an energy intensity improvement of 4% per year on average to 2030, or about 3 times that achieved over the past 2 decades. It will require a major increase in renewable energy use, energy efficiency, and clean energy innovations, while fossil fuels will have to shrink to about one-fifth of the energy supply by 2050, from about four-fifths today. Moreover, the net zero scenario requires that global energy demand by 2050 fall by 8%, posing a considerable challenge with 2 billion additional people on the planet. Emissions from industry, transport, and buildings will have to fall by 95% by 2050, requiring major efforts to build new and retool existing infrastructure. 

Investments associated with the shift toward net zero are massive. 

The IEA study uses modeling undertaken with the International Monetary Fund to calculate annual investment requirements for the energy sector. It concludes that such investments will need to more than double to $5 trillion by 2030, from about $2.3 trillion currently. On the positive side, this should add 0.4% to annual global GDP growth.

snippet.text:
The International Energy Agency (IEA 2021) conducted a comprehensive study on the net zero transition for the energy sector, which accounts for three-fourths of greenhouse gases. The influential study put forward three main scenarios: (i) Stated Policy Scenario, including specific plans already in place or announced by governments; (ii) Announcement Pledges Case, where all announced national zero pledges were assumed to be achieved on time; and (iii) Net Zero Scenario by 2050, which forms the core of the analysis in the paper. The Stated Policy Scenario would lead global temperatures to rise 2.7°C, while the rise in the Pledges Case scenarios would be 2.1°C (each with a 50% probability). Net zero would be consistent with a 1.5°C rise (with a 50% probability). 

The study's net zero scenario stipulates the necessary conditions for the global energy sector to reach net zero emissions by 2050. 17 The policy challenges are daunting. The net zero pathway assumes the world economy in 2030 will be two-fifths larger than today but will use 7% less energy, requiring an energy intensity improvement of 4% per year on average to 2030, or about 3 times that achieved over the past 2 decades. It will require a major increase in renewable energy use, energy efficiency, and clean energy innovations, while fossil fuels will have to shrink to about one-fifth of the energy supply by 2050, from about four-fifths today. Moreover, the net zero scenario requires that global energy demand by 2050 fall by 8%, posing a considerable challenge with 2 billion additional people on the planet. Emissions from industry, transport, and buildings will have to fall by 95% by 2050, requiring major efforts to build new and retool existing infrastructure. 

Investments associated with the shift toward net zero are massive. 

The IEA study uses modeling undertaken with the International Monetary Fund to calculate annual investment requirements for the energy sector. It concludes that such investments will need to more than double to $5 trillion by 2030, from about $2.3 trillion currently. On the positive side, this should add 0.4% to annual global GDP growth.

Title: Challenges and opportunities of the full phase-out of fossil fuels under the 1.5 °C goal
Snippet: The COP28 decision called for transitioning away from fossil fuels, sparking a growing interest in their full phase-out. However, energy system transformation pathways towards a phase-out of fossil fuels, which may reduce the reliance on carbon dioxide removal to meet the 1.5 °C goal, remain unclear. Here, we employ two global energy system models to explore energy system transformations and the challenges and opportunities associated with attaining a full phase-out of fossil fuels. We found that phasing out fossil fuels by 2050 would require accelerating direct and indirect electrification, involving 1.6–1.8-fold increases in power generation compared to the conventional cost-effective 1.5 °C pathways. This transition from cost-effective to fossil fuel phase-out pathways would increase energy supply investments by up to 34% over this century and require accelerated deployment of solar and wind power, as well as electrolysers. Despite opportunities including lower reliance on carbon dioxide removal and increasing probability of returning to 1.5 °C after temperature overshoot, these additional requirements imply that international society must approach the transition towards zero-fossil energy systems with strong determination. There is a lack of energy system transformation pathways required to achieve a full phase-out of fossil fuels by 2050 in the literature. This paper finds it requires rapid electrification and 1.6–1.8-fold increases in power generation compared to cost-effective 1.5 °C pathways.

Title: Challenges and opportunities of the full phase-out of fossil fuels under the 1.5 °C goal
Snippet: Although the final decision does not explicitly mention a full phase-out, momentum is growing for the phase-out of fossil fuels to become a key focus of climate policies moving forward from COP28. Notably, in 2024, the Group of Seven (G7) committed to phasing out existing unabated coal power generation during the first half of the 2030s 4 , and the Group of Twenty (G20) leaders fully subscribed to the outcome of COP28, in particular the UAE Consensus and the GST-1 5 . 

The decarbonisation and defossilisation of energy systems could follow different energy transformation pathways. Title: Challenges and opportunities of the full phase-out of fossil fuels under the 1.5 °C goal
Snippet: The COP28 decision called for transitioning away from fossil fuels, sparking a growing interest in their full phase-out. However, energy system transformation pathways towards a phase-out of fossil fuels, which may reduce the reliance on carbon dioxide removal to meet the 1.5 °C goal, remain unclear. Here, we employ two global energy system models to explore energy system transformations and the challenges and opportunities associated with attaining a full phase-out of fossil fuels. We found that phasing out fossil fuels by 2050 would require accelerating direct and indirect electrification, involving 1.6-1.8-fold increases in power generation compared to the conventional costeffective 1.5 °C pathways. This transition from cost-effective to fossil fuel phase-out pathways would increase energy supply investments by up to 34% over this century and require accelerated deployment of solar and wind power, as well as electrolysers. Despite opportunities including lower reliance on carbon dioxide removal and increasing probability of returning to 1.5 °C after temperature overshoot, these additional requirements imply that international society must approach the transition towards zero-fossil energy systems with strong determination. 

Limiting global warming to well below 2 °C, and pursuing efforts to return to 1.5 °C after temporary overshoot by the end of the century in line with the Paris Agreement, requires a rapid reduction of fossil fuel contributions to the energy system 1,2 . The final decision of the first Global Stocktake (GST-1) at the 2023 United Nations Conference of the Parties (COP28) highlighted the necessity for urgent action to address the climate crisis, given that the Parties are not on track to achieve the long-term goals of the Paris Agreement 3 . A key achievement of the GST-1 decision was that it called for all Parties to contribute to global efforts, particularly transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems. Although the final decision does not explicitly mention a full phase-out, momentum is growing for the phase-out of fossil fuels to become a key focus of climate policies moving forward from COP28.

Title: The Changing Role of Nuclear Power in the European Union: Reflections from Official Scenarios Released before and after the Fukushima Daiichi Accident
Snippet: Regarding electricity demand, as can be seen in Figure 6 and Figure 7, all scenarios from the Prognos (2011) study and scenarios published directly after the Fukushima accident suggest that electricity demand could rise steadily until 2030, but by varying degrees due to the varied population growth expected by the authors. However, the decarbonisation of electricity generation and the expected rate of substitution towards electricity for fossil fuels in transportation and heating could play a significant role in the increase of total electricity demand. Despite the fact that changes in the development of electricity generation and in its structure highly depend on the different assumptions used in the scenarios regarding renewable energy targets, GHG targets, limitations of new plant constructions and their cost structure, renewable energy sources are expected to play a major role across all scenarios in delivering electricity in 2050. In almost all the scenarios from Prognos (2011) and those released after the Fukushima accident, wind power technologies provide the major share of electricity from renewable sources. Electricity generation from fossil fuel sources will decline by 2050, according to all scenarios being analysed. According to the EU's Energy Roadmap 2050 (EC 2011), the share of oil in net electricity generation will decline from 30% (in 2005) to 2.1-15.2% by 2050, while in all scenarios of EU Roadmap 2050 the share of gas and coal in power generation will also decrease by 2050 compared to 2005, to 15.1-19.5% and 2.1-15.2% respectively. In nearly in all scenarios (with the exceptions of Eurelectric's Power Choices scenario, ECF's 40% RES scenario, and EU's Reference scenario) renewable energy sources contribute more to electricity supply in 2050 than fossil fuels or nuclear power; however, the role of Carbon Capture and Storage varies across the scenarios (Förster et al. 2012).

In 2030, when the transition is in the intermediate phase, fossil fuels are still a significant component, especially for primary energy.On the other hand, the decline of coal in the Net Zero scenario is significant in all models (AIM/Hub and TIMES retain some coal-fired power generation in 2030, but the decline is appreciable).The exact timing of the phase-out of coal power generation without CCS varies across models, ranging from 2030 to after 2050 (although it is virtually eliminated in all models by that year) (see figure ESM 6).Coal without CCS is zero or negligible in all models.

In all models, the total electricity generation increases from the Baseline to the Low Carbon (80%) to the Net Zero scenario while fossil fuels decrease significantly.The exact composition varies considerably.For instance, the share of variable renewable energy (VRE) sources ranges from 38% in the IEEJ_NE model to 72% in the AIM/Technology model.

On the demand side, final energy decreases slightly between the Low Carbon (80%) and Net Zero scenarios.In the AIM/Hub and IEEJ models, there is a significant drop in final energy compared to the Baseline scenario.The models show the dominance of electricity by 2050 (figure 5).Hydrogen makes some inroads in three models, especially for the Net Zero scenario.(Note that the AIM/Hub model used in this study does not represent hydrogen as a final energy carrier.)

Title: Scales and Consequences of Deep Decarbonization of the Russian Electric Power Industry
Snippet: In the base scenario, in 2050, the demand of power plants for fuel will remain slightly higher than it was in 2019, with retaining the share of gas in the structure of this demand at a level of 72-73%. In the intensive scenario, the total consumption of fossil fuel at TPPs in 2050 will be by 28.0% lower than the reporting level. The demand for gas after 2035 will decrease more slowly than the total fuel consumption, and it will be by only 9.4% smaller by 2050 than it was in 2019. 

The change in the amounts and structure of using fossil fuel will also determine the dynamics of СО 2 emissions from power plants in the final analysis (see Table 6). In the base scenario, the amounts of emissions vary synchronously with the fuel consumption dynamics: the peak of emission is reached by 2035 (the increase by 12.3% with respect to the level in 2019); with the further decrease, the emissions will return by 2050 to the values of the reporting level. In the intensive scenario, the peak of emission will be reached earlier-in 2030 (with the increase by 8.2% with respect to 2019), and the subsequent reduction of annual СО 2 emissions will go more rapidly than the decrease of fossil fuel consumption at TPPs. As a result, in this scenario, the СО 2 emissions from power plants in 2050 will be by 39% lower than the reporting level and by almost 40% lower than in the base scenario. 

The technological changes in the generating capacity mix are reflected to a larger extent on the use of fuel for electricity production. Therefore, the СО 2 emissions connected with fuel consumption for electricity production will decrease, in both scenarios, more rapidly than the total amount of СО 2 emission from power plants. The carbon intensity of electricity production, which is the specific indicator of emissions, will show a still more rapid decrease. Since the growth of electricity production even in the base scenario will be noticeably faster than the dynamics of СО 2 emissions entailing this production, the carbon intensity of electricity production will by 2030 remain at the reporting level of 2019 and it will decrease by 35% by 2050.

snippet.text: Regarding electricity demand, as can be seen in Figure 6 and Figure 7, all scenarios from the Prognos (2011) study and scenarios published directly after the Fukushima accident suggest that electricity demand could rise steadily until 2030, but by varying degrees due to the varied population growth expected by the authors. However, the decarbonisation of electricity generation and the expected rate of substitution towards electricity for fossil fuels in transportation and heating could play a significant role in the increase of total electricity demand. Despite the fact that changes in the development of electricity generation and in its structure highly depend on the different assumptions used in the scenarios regarding renewable energy targets, GHG targets, limitations of new plant constructions and their cost structure, renewable energy sources are expected to play a major role across all scenarios in delivering electricity in 2050. In almost all the scenarios from Prognos (2011) and those released after the Fukushima accident, wind power technologies provide the major share of electricity from renewable sources. Electricity generation from fossil fuel sources will decline by 2050, according to all scenarios being analysed. According to the EU's Energy Roadmap 2050 (EC 2011), the share of oil in net electricity generation will decline from 30% (in 2005) to 2.1-15.2% by 2050, while in all scenarios of EU Roadmap 2050 the share of gas and coal in power generation will also decrease by 2050 compared to 2005, to 15.1-19.5% and 2.1-15.2% respectively. In nearly in all scenarios (with the exceptions of Eurelectric's Power Choices scenario, ECF's 40% RES scenario, and EU's Reference scenario) renewable energy sources contribute more to electricity supply in 2050 than fossil fuels or nuclear power; however, the role of Carbon Capture and Storage varies across the scenarios (Förster et al. 2012).

The mean is 1,712 TWh, and thus about one-third below today's value. Thereby, the share of fossil fuels decrease and the electricity share increases. 

Electricity demand is expected to increase significantly in most scenarios, especially in the long term (2020: 553 TWh; mean 2030: 692 TWh; mean 2050: 958 TWh). The lowest number is 510 TWh/a in the scenarios Prognos PtX 80 and 95 in 2030. In contrast, the highest value for 2030 is reached in scenarios LBST H2-80% and LBST H2-95%. For 2050, the demand for electricity in Prognos PtX 80 and 95 remains similarly low as in 2030 (521 TWh). In LBST H2-95%, ISE Reference and ISE Inertia, however, this demand is higher than 1,400 TWh/a. It is because electricity is needed either directly for end-use applications or indirectly to produce hydrogen via electrolysis. However, there are exceptions. The decisive factor for the level of electricity demand is how much synthetic fuels are imported. In studies that foresee a high share of such imports, the electricity demand is lower. In all examined scenarios, the share of coal-fired electricity is declining significantly by 2030 or is already at zero. Instead, gas and renewable energies are becoming more critical. To achieve the climate targets, electricity will increasingly be produced from renewable energies. In 2050, the share of renewables in the electricity sector exceeds 70% in all scenarios and thus represents by far the most important type of power generation. The mean share is 90%, whereby dena Baseline indicates the lowest share at 72%, while in other scenarios even a share of 100% is reached. 

In terms of hydrogen, various scenarios do not foresee a broad use by 2030.

judgment.criterion_reasoning: The answer comprehensively discusses specific strategies, technologies, and pathways for reducing global dependence on oil and gas in the context of environmental sustainability. It covers: (1) renewable energy adoption with specific targets (70-85% renewable electricity by 2050), (2) electrification of transport, buildings, and industry, (3) energy efficiency improvements (4% annual energy intensity gains through 2030), (4) hydrogen and alternative fuels for hard-to-abate sectors, (5) investment frameworks ($5 trillion annually by 2030), (6) policy frameworks including COP28 commitments and carbon pricing, and (7) specific near-term milestones and timelines. The answer systematically addresses the environmental necessity through carbon budget constraints and temperature targets (1.5-2°C).
other_issues: Reference [4] appears to be misused: The cited snippet discusses projections showing continued fossil fuel dominance and modest changes, yet the answer presents this as supporting the transition narrative. The source actually shows what happens if policies DON'T change ('at best if policies and investment plans do not change, GHG emissions will at best remain at current levels'), which contradicts how it's positioned in the answer.

Reference [7] citation usage is problematic: The answer states 'Transport electrification and biofuel shares rise modestly by 2040 in some scenarios' [7], but the cited snippet actually describes scenarios that are 'hardly in line with the targets of the Paris Agreement' with continued fossil fuel dominance (73-90% fossil fuels in 2040). This is presented neutrally rather than as a cautionary counterpoint.

Minor structural issue: The answer occasionally uses references to support contrasting points (business-as-usual vs. net-zero pathways) without clearly distinguishing which scenario is being discussed, potentially confusing readers about whether cited figures represent desired targets or problematic baselines.

Reference [11] discusses biofuels specifically in the context of IEA's Blue Map 2050, but the answer uses it primarily to cite the 450 ppm target and emission reduction percentages, which is accurate but doesn't leverage the biofuel-specific content that could strengthen the alternative fuels discussion.
judgment.summary: The answer strongly satisfies the verification criterion by providing detailed, well-structured coverage of strategies, technologies, and pathways for reducing fossil fuel dependence. However, there are notable issues with how some references are deployed, particularly [4] and [7], which describe business-as-usual or inadequate scenarios but are presented in ways that could mislead readers about their actual content. The factual claims appear accurate when traced to sources, but contextual framing needs improvement to distinguish between aspirational pathways and cautionary baseline scenarios.

harder.brainstorming: The seed is broad and asks about the global prospect of reducing fossil fuel dependence. A retrieval system can easily survey environmental impacts, renewable energy adoption rates, and policy trends. To increase difficulty, I could require complex multi-variable reasoning about interconnected economic, political, and technological factors. Alternatively, I could embed a constraint that forces the system to distinguish between what's environmentally necessary versus what's economically/politically feasible—most papers argue for necessity but this conflates 'should happen' with 'will happen.' The strongest approach: require the system to evaluate whether the 'environmental necessity' framing itself oversimplifies by ignoring that necessity doesn't guarantee feasibility, forcing analysis of the gap between normative claims and predictive ones.
harder.chosen_strategy: Embed a critical evaluation constraint that requires distinguishing between normative environmental necessity claims versus positive empirical predictions about what will actually occur. The system must recognize that papers making necessity arguments (climate targets require X) use different evidence and logic than papers predicting feasibility (current trajectories suggest Y), and these often diverge. This requires evaluating the strength of the assumption that necessity drives outcomes.
harder.updated_question: Does the environmental necessity of reducing oil and gas dependence predict its actual global feasibility by 2050?
harder.why_harder: Climate and energy literature contains abundant papers arguing what's environmentally necessary (IPCC pathways, carbon budgets) and separate papers analyzing what's economically/politically feasible (IEA scenarios, technology adoption curves, geopolitical constraints). A retrieval-strong system will find both types but struggle with the meta-analytical task of evaluating whether necessity-claims actually function as valid predictors of feasibility. This requires recognizing that normative arguments ('must happen to avoid 2°C warming') and positive predictions ('will happen given current policies/economics') rely on fundamentally different evidence bases, and that many necessity-focused papers explicitly acknowledge a feasibility gap rather than claiming necessity ensures achievement.
harder.verification_criterion: The answer must explicitly distinguish between environmental necessity arguments (what reduction levels climate science says are required) and feasibility projections (what reduction levels energy economics/policy analysis predicts will occur), and must directly address whether one predicts the other—either by showing necessity does drive feasible outcomes through specific mechanisms with evidence, or by identifying a gap where necessity claims exceed feasibility projections. Fails if it conflates the two by treating necessity arguments as though they constitute evidence of feasibility, or if it surveys necessity and feasibility literature separately without analyzing their relationship.

Below, we synthesize how necessity predicts feasibility, where evidence supports global feasibility by 2050, and where deeper constraints remain.

Environmental necessity through 2050
Limiting warming to “well below 2°C” and pursuing 1.5°C requires global net‑zero greenhouse gas emissions around or after 2050, which in practice means rapidly decarbonizing energy, transport, buildings, and industry. <cite id="688848c7-0">Pathways without overshoot require a rapid worldwide energy transition with pronounced changes in the next two decades, including faster electrification, efficiency gains, a higher share of low‑emission electricity (70–85% by 2050), and near‑zero coal and very low gas shares</cite>. <cite id="688848c7-3">Recent analyses propose halving CO2 emissions every decade from 2020 up to 2050 and ramping up carbon removal thereafter to reach net zero after 2050</cite>. <cite id="688848c7-4">IPCC emphasizes a 45% fall in global CO2 emissions by 2030 and net zero around 2050, with national frameworks aligning sectoral reductions accordingly</cite>. These targets translate directly into dependence on oil and gas declining toward a small residual role, with electrification, fuels with carbon removal, and materials/feedstock decarbonization.

What “feasible by 2050” implies in practice
Global feasibility hinges on scaling renewables and electrification, enabling technologies, and efficiency upgrades at rates consistent with integrated assessment model pathways.

- Scale of renewable buildout and electrification. <cite id="25812453-0">The IEA Net Zero pathway assumes the world economy is 20% larger in 2030 than today but uses 7% less energy, requiring 4% annual energy intensity improvement to 2030 and major increases in renewable energy, energy efficiency, and clean innovation; fossil fuels fall to about one‑fifth of energy by 2050, with energy demand down 8% despite population and activity growth</cite>. <cite id="25812453-4">Under IEA Net Zero, ~50% of energy supply becomes electricity by 2050, with 88% of that from wind and solar, implying annual wind additions of ~390 GW by 2030 (up from ~114 GW in 2020) and ~8,000 GW by 2050</cite>. <cite id="688848c7-0">Pathways converge on 70–85% renewable electricity by 2050, with gas near zero and coal near zero</cite>. <cite id="25812453-2">Tripling renewable capacity by 2030 is central; advanced economies and China can deliver ~85% of required renewable capacity under existing policies, but developing countries need stronger policies and international support to close the gap</cite>. These rates imply feasibility if current learning‑by‑doing accelerates, supply chains mature, and policies create stable demand signals and grid flexibility.

- Sectoral substitution and enabling technologies. <cite id="688848c7-1">Fossil fuels will continue to play an indispensable role through 2050 for certain carbon‑embodied products and polymers, requiring substantial carbon capture deployment (4 Gt CO2 in 2035 rising to 7.6 Gt in 2050) and electrification across sectors</cite>. <cite id="922c8993-3">Hydrogen and CCUS play pivotal roles post‑2030, but their realization hinges on significant investments in production, transmission, and distribution; announced electrolysis projects cover ~70% of 2030 demand and announced CCUS ~40% of global needs, implying policy‑driven demand creation is essential</cite>. <cite id="688848c7-1">Nuclear and fossil with CCS can serve as bridges if acceptable, but pathways increasingly rely on renewables as the primary supply</cite>. <cite id="25812453-3">IEA highlights rapid progress in solar PV and BEVs and estimates the world can deliver ~35% fossil fuel emission cuts by 2030 under heightened policy action</cite>.

- Methane and near‑term oil & gas demand. <cite id="922c8993-1">Rapid methane mitigation in oil and gas delivers outsized climate benefits: oil and gas supply chain measures alone account for ~80% of avoided warming from economically feasible actions, with leak detection and repair plus company leakage commitments avoiding ~0.1°C by midcentury and ~0.2°C by 2100 versus a no‑action baseline</cite>. <cite id="922c8993-2">Full deployment of available methane measures by 2030 can slow warming by >25% over the next decades, preventing ~0.1°C in 2050 and ~0.5°C in 2100 relative to slow action, with oil and gas dominating economically feasible abatement</cite>. <cite id="922c8993-0">An “rapid action” US scenario reduces methane emission factors to 31% of current levels by 2030 (69% abatement), consistent with IEA abatement potential estimates and aligned with the Global Methane Pledge for upstream leakage</cite>. <cite id="922c8993-4">Even with steep gas demand declines, residual methane emissions along a gas value chain can exceed emissions of scenarios with higher gas use, underscoring that methane abatement is essential to avoid net warming</cite>. Together, these results suggest oil and gas demand can be rapidly curbed by improving efficiency, electrifying end uses, and cutting methane at the margin, while residual supply roles are compensated by renewables, hydrogen, and CCUS.

- Carbon budget and residual emissions. <cite id="688848c7-2">IPCC estimates of remaining CO2 budgets range from 315–755 Gt CO2 from 2018 to stay within 1.5–2°C, translating into tight residual carbon budgets after 2030–2040</cite>. <cite id="688848c7-0">Pathways that avoid overshoot require net‑zero across all sectors by 2050, implying that residual oil and gas use must be matched by carbon removal technologies or zero‑carbon substitutes</cite>. <cite id="688848c7-0">Limited overshoot pathways increasingly rely on rapid electrification and efficiency to shrink absolute fossil demand, with residual gas and coal phased to near zero by 2050</cite>. Thus feasibility depends on both supply decarbonization and credible, scalable removal/offset policies for residuals.

Several well‑identified constraints can make “feasible in principle” more or less “achievable by 2050” at the global scale.

- Infrastructure lifetimes and stranded assets. <cite id="fd1e4b01-0">Paris‑aligned scenarios in Latin America imply premature retirement of 60–128 GW of fossil power (15–33% of 2015 capacity) by 2050, with natural gas without CCS comprising the largest fraction of stranded capacity in fast mitigation, challenging the viability of gas as a bridge</cite>. <cite id="fd1e4b01-1">Offshore oil and gas platforms typically reach end‑of‑life within ~30 years; policy shifts (e.g., Denmark’s 2020 moratorium on new exploration) force closure by 2050, raising decommissioning costs and motivating repurposing of platforms for offshore wind or hydrogen</cite>. <cite id="fd1e4b01-2">The global oil and gas infrastructure stock is worth ~$25 trillion and substantial shale reserves are economically valuable; shifts in policy and technology can strand assets and create carbon lock‑in, with path‑dependent incentives to fully exploit sunk costs</cite>. <cite id="fd1e4b01-3">Global stranded asset losses in upstream oil and gas may exceed $1 trillion under plausible policy changes, with risk concentrated among private investors in OECD countries via complex ownership networks</cite>. <cite id="fd1e4b01-4">Carbon lock‑in persists because firms pursue full‑lifetime use of assets; governments and companies still plan to extract far more than 1.5°C is consistent with, and fossil subsidies hit $1 trillion in 2022</cite>. These dynamics imply feasibility is higher where policy creates early demand pull (e.g., carbon pricing, renewable mandates, hydrogen pipelines), aligns asset retirements with climate pathways, and mitigates stranded‑asset risk through just‑transition and investment guarantees.

- Finance and investment scale. <cite id="25812453-0">Global energy investments must more than double to ~$5 trillion per year by 2030 (from ~$2.3 trillion today), with modeling suggesting GDP gains of ~0.4% per year due to clean energy deployment</cite>. <cite id="688848c7-1">Meeting net‑zero requires that about half of fossil fuels be equipped with carbon capture (4 Gt CO2 in 2035, 7.6 Gt in 2050), implying significant capital needs for capture and storage networks</cite>. <cite id="922c8993-3">Hydrogen supply chains and CCUS also require ~70% of 2030 electrolysis capacity and ~40% of CCUS projects already announced to meet net‑zero pathways, with the remainder dependent on policy‑driven demand and infrastructure build‑out</cite>. While financing is feasible in principle given positive expected returns and macroeconomic co‑benefits, risks include cost inflation, supply chain bottlenecks, and stranded‑portfolio concerns that raise capital costs.

- Equity, governance, and distributional feasibility. <cite id="28593032-0">Decarbonization is unevenly distributed across regions, with many fossil‑intensive economies facing lock‑in and stranded assets, underscoring that policy design, technology transfer, and finance are pivotal to equitable transitions</cite>. <cite id="fd1e4b01-3">Because most stranded‑asset risk is held by OECD investors and pension funds, global governance mechanisms must align incentives so that oil and gas phase‑out is managed to limit systemic financial shocks and support fair adjustment</cite>. <cite id="25812453-2">Developing countries can reach much of the renewable build‑out needed by 2050 under existing policies, but accelerated policy measures and stronger international support are essential to close remaining gaps</cite>.

Taken together, the evidence supports a conditional “yes.” The climate targets set a clear direction and magnitude of change required in oil and gas use by 2050, and modeling indicates that these changes are technically achievable if deployment scales at unprecedented rates, methane is rapidly abated, and enabling infrastructure (electricity grids, hydrogen, CCUS) is built in tandem with demand‑side measures. <cite id="688848c7-0">Net‑zero by 2050 implies all fossil fuel consumption must be replaced by zero‑carbon alternatives, requiring rapid, worldwide transformation</cite> <cite id="25812453-0">IEA pathways to net zero in the energy sector show fossil fuels shrinking to ~one‑fifth of energy supply by 2050 alongside ~$5 trillion/year investments by 2030 and 8% lower total energy use by 2050</cite> <cite id="922c8993-1">Rapid methane mitigation in oil and gas alone can prevent ~0.1°C by midcentury and ~0.2°C by 2100 versus no‑action, accelerating demand reduction</cite> <cite id="25812453-4">Achieving ~50% electricity share by 2050 with 88% wind and solar implies feasible deployment trajectories if policy and supply chains enable ~390 GW/year of wind additions by 2030</cite>. However, feasibility is not guaranteed: <cite id="fd1e4b01-0">Paris‑aligned pathways imply large‑scale premature retirements of fossil plants, with gas without CCS especially vulnerable, creating stranded‑asset and reliability risks</cite> <cite id="fd1e4b01-3">Stranded asset losses could exceed $1 trillion in upstream oil and gas, concentrated in the Global North</cite> <cite id="25812453-0">Energy intensity must improve at roughly triple the historical pace to 2030, and global demand must fall despite rising activity</cite>. These constraints make feasibility contingent on governance and finance that de‑risk transitions, align asset retirements with climate targets, and mobilize capital at the necessary scale.

Practical implications for 2050
- Oil and gas supply: <cite id="922c8993-2">Full methane abatement by 2030 cuts projected warming by more than a quarter over the next decades and reduces warming by 0.1–0.5°C by 2050–2100</cite>, making supply more climate‑compatible and extending asset lives where repurposed (e.g., offshore wind/hydrogen on oil platforms). <cite id="fd1e4b01-1">Repurposing mature oil and gas platforms to renewables can extend asset lifetimes and reduce stranded costs</cite>. <cite id="922c8993-4">Even large declines in gas use can yield higher total methane emissions if abatement is insufficient, so regulatory methane caps and verification are essential</cite>.
- Renewable energy: <cite id="25812453-2">Advanced economies and China can supply most of the renewable capacity required by 2050 under existing policies, with international support critical for developing nations</cite>. <cite id="688848c7-0">Pathways converge on 70–85% renewable electricity with very low coal and near-zero gas, implying feasibility if transmission, storage, and flexibility are scaled</cite>.
- Demand‑side electrification and fuels: <cite id="25812453-3">IEA finds rapid progress in solar and BEVs and indicates ~35% fossil fuel emission cuts by 2030 are deliverable under accelerated policies</cite>. <cite id="688848c7-1">Electrification of end uses and materials/feedstock decarbonization reduce dependence on oil and gas, while CCUS covers residual emissions</cite>.

Bottom line
Environmental necessity (45% emissions cut by 2030 and net zero by 2050) predicts that global oil and gas dependence must fall dramatically by 2050, and modeling shows such global feasibility is attainable if deployment rates, methane abatement, and enabling infrastructure scale rapidly and finance and governance de‑risk transitions. <cite id="688848c7-0">Net‑zero by 2050 requires replacing fossil fuels with zero‑carbon alternatives across all sectors</cite> <cite id="25812453-0">IEA pathways show fossil shares falling to ~20% of energy by 2050 with unprecedented investment and efficiency gains</cite> <cite id="922c8993-1">Methane abatement in oil and gas yields large, low‑cost near‑term climate benefits</cite> <cite id="fd1e4b01-0">Paris‑aligned transitions imply large‑scale retirements and stranded assets, especially for gas without CCS, necessitating proactive policy design</cite> <cite id="fd1e4b01-3">Global stranded asset losses could exceed $1 trillion, concentrated among OECD investors, underscoring systemic risks and the need for coordinated transition management</cite>. The gap between what is necessary and what is predicted to be feasible narrows where methane is rapidly cut, assets are retired justly, finance is mobilized, and policies create stable demand for clean energy and hydrogen/CCUS by 2030, increasing confidence that global oil and gas dependence can be reduced in line with 2050 climate goals.

Snippet: The Oil & Gas (O&G) sector is facing many challenges. These include international climate frameworks such as the Paris Agreement, consistently low crude oil prices together and the foreseeable End Of Life (EOL) of many O&G assets. On the one hand, there is need to clarify the implications of the wider energy transition on existing O&G operations. On the other hand, much offshore infrastructure is reaching or will soon reach (e.g. within 30 years) the end of its economically operational lifetime. The decision of the Danish Government in December 2020 to cancel new O&G explorations in the Danish North Sea means all existing production must have ceased by 2050. Faced with potentially very high decommissioning costs for this infrastructure, the O&G sector may benefit from a partial or complete repurposing of this infrastructure, during and/or after its operational lifetime. This report presents the findings of a feasibility study about exploiting synergies between offshore O&G and renewable energy activities in the Danish Underground Consortium (DUC) region of the North Sea. The objective was to develop a roadmap for this sector out to 2050. The project was funded by the DHRTC alongside six other projects exploring the technical and economic feasibility of alternative uses for existing O&G infrastructure. The research was carried out from September 2020 to January 2021 between the School of Engineering, University of Aberdeen, and the Division of Sustainability, DTU Management, Technical University of Denmark. The very short timeframe and small project team mean that the analysis is relatively high-level, requiring many simplifying assumptions and resulting in some important technical details being overlooked and left for future research. For this reason, this report should be understood as a starting point for further and more detailed analysis, rather than a definitive roadmap for the sector.

On the other hand, the interlocking web of infrastructure, technologies and institutions underpinning the existing fossil fuel-based system creates a path-dependent process of 'carbon lock-in' which inhibits transitions toward low-carbon alternatives (Seto et al., 2016). 

According to available geological estimates, there are large reserves of recoverable shale oil and gas in the United States, Canada and worldwide. Global estimates for shale oil are 345 billion barrels (Bbbl) and for shale gas are at least 100 trillion cubic ft 3 (Tcf); estimates for US recoverable shale oil are 58 Bbbl and estimated shale gas reserves are 600-1000 Tcf (Jackson et al., 2014, 329). 

Given the 345 Bbbl shale-oil reserves at the price of oil US$100/ barrel, shale-oil reserves are worth US$35 trillion (Jackson et al., 2014, 329). Snippet: The distribution of ownership of transition risk associated with stranded fossil-fuel assets remains poorly understood. We calculate that global stranded assets as present value of future lost profits in the upstream oil and gas sector exceed US$1 trillion under plausible changes in expectations about the effects of climate policy. We trace the equity risk ownership from 43,439 oil and gas production assets through a global equity network of 1.8 million companies to their ultimate owners. Most of the market risk falls on private investors, overwhelmingly in OECD countries, including substantial exposure through pension funds and financial markets. The ownership distribution reveals an international net transfer of more than 15% of global stranded asset risk to OECD-based investors. Rich country stakeholders therefore have a major stake in how the transition in oil and gas production is managed, as ongoing supporters of the fossil-fuel economy and potentially exposed owners of stranded assets. The necessary and rapid transition to a low-carbon economy will lead to massive stranded assets, which could risk the stability of financial markets and the economy. Through a global equity network, most risk and responsibility is owned by investors, such as pension funds, in developed countries.
