- Scale of renewable buildout and electrification. <cite id="25812453-0">The IEA Net Zero pathway assumes the world economy is 20% larger in 2030 than today but uses 7% less energy, requiring 4% annual energy intensity improvement to 2030 and major increases in renewable energy, energy efficiency, and clean innovation; fossil fuels fall to about one‑fifth of energy by 2050, with energy demand down 8% despite population and activity growth</cite>. <cite id="25812453-4">Under IEA Net Zero, ~50% of energy supply becomes electricity by 2050, with 88% of that from wind and solar, implying annual wind additions of ~390 GW by 2030 (up from ~114 GW in 2020) and ~8,000 GW by 2050</cite>. <cite id="688848c7-0">Pathways converge on 70–85% renewable electricity by 2050, with gas near zero and coal near zero</cite>. <cite id="25812453-2">Tripling renewable capacity by 2030 is central; advanced economies and China can deliver ~85% of required renewable capacity under existing policies, but developing countries need stronger policies and international support to close the gap</cite>. These rates imply feasibility if current learning‑by‑doing accelerates, supply chains mature, and policies create stable demand signals and grid flexibility.

- Sectoral substitution and enabling technologies. <cite id="688848c7-1">Fossil fuels will continue to play an indispensable role through 2050 for certain carbon‑embodied products and polymers, requiring substantial carbon capture deployment (4 Gt CO2 in 2035 rising to 7.6 Gt in 2050) and electrification across sectors</cite>. <cite id="922c8993-3">Hydrogen and CCUS play pivotal roles post‑2030, but their realization hinges on significant investments in production, transmission, and distribution; announced electrolysis projects cover ~70% of 2030 demand and announced CCUS ~40% of global needs, implying policy‑driven demand creation is essential</cite>. <cite id="688848c7-1">Nuclear and fossil with CCS can serve as bridges if acceptable, but pathways increasingly rely on renewables as the primary supply</cite>. <cite id="25812453-3">IEA highlights rapid progress in solar PV and BEVs and estimates the world can deliver ~35% fossil fuel emission cuts by 2030 under heightened policy action</cite>.

- Methane and near‑term oil & gas demand. <cite id="922c8993-1">Rapid methane mitigation in oil and gas delivers outsized climate benefits: oil and gas supply chain measures alone account for ~80% of avoided warming from economically feasible actions, with leak detection and repair plus company leakage commitments avoiding ~0.1°C by midcentury and ~0.2°C by 2100 versus a no‑action baseline</cite>. <cite id="922c8993-2">Full deployment of available methane measures by 2030 can slow warming by >25% over the next decades, preventing ~0.1°C in 2050 and ~0.5°C in 2100 relative to slow action, with oil and gas dominating economically feasible abatement</cite>. <cite id="922c8993-0">An “rapid action” US scenario reduces methane emission factors to 31% of current levels by 2030 (69% abatement), consistent with IEA abatement potential estimates and aligned with the Global Methane Pledge for upstream leakage</cite>. <cite id="922c8993-4">Even with steep gas demand declines, residual methane emissions along a gas value chain can exceed emissions of scenarios with higher gas use, underscoring that methane abatement is essential to avoid net warming</cite>. Together, these results suggest oil and gas demand can be rapidly curbed by improving efficiency, electrifying end uses, and cutting methane at the margin, while residual supply roles are compensated by renewables, hydrogen, and CCUS.

- Carbon budget and residual emissions. <cite id="688848c7-2">IPCC estimates of remaining CO2 budgets range from 315–755 Gt CO2 from 2018 to stay within 1.5–2°C, translating into tight residual carbon budgets after 2030–2040</cite>. <cite id="688848c7-0">Pathways that avoid overshoot require net‑zero across all sectors by 2050, implying that residual oil and gas use must be matched by carbon removal technologies or zero‑carbon substitutes</cite>. <cite id="688848c7-0">Limited overshoot pathways increasingly rely on rapid electrification and efficiency to shrink absolute fossil demand, with residual gas and coal phased to near zero by 2050</cite>. Thus feasibility depends on both supply decarbonization and credible, scalable removal/offset policies for residuals.

Constraints and risks to global feasibility
Several well‑identified constraints can make “feasible in principle” more or less “achievable by 2050” at the global scale.

- Infrastructure lifetimes and stranded assets. <cite id="fd1e4b01-0">Paris‑aligned scenarios in Latin America imply premature retirement of 60–128 GW of fossil power (15–33% of 2015 capacity) by 2050, with natural gas without CCS comprising the largest fraction of stranded capacity in fast mitigation, challenging the viability of gas as a bridge</cite>. <cite id="fd1e4b01-1">Offshore oil and gas platforms typically reach end‑of‑life within ~30 years; policy shifts (e.g., Denmark’s 2020 moratorium on new exploration) force closure by 2050, raising decommissioning costs and motivating repurposing of platforms for offshore wind or hydrogen</cite>. <cite id="fd1e4b01-2">The global oil and gas infrastructure stock is worth ~$25 trillion and substantial shale reserves are economically valuable; shifts in policy and technology can strand assets and create carbon lock‑in, with path‑dependent incentives to fully exploit sunk costs</cite>. <cite id="fd1e4b01-3">Global stranded asset losses in upstream oil and gas may exceed $1 trillion under plausible policy changes, with risk concentrated among private investors in OECD countries via complex ownership networks</cite>. <cite id="fd1e4b01-4">Carbon lock‑in persists because firms pursue full‑lifetime use of assets; governments and companies still plan to extract far more than 1.5°C is consistent with, and fossil subsidies hit $1 trillion in 2022</cite>. These dynamics imply feasibility is higher where policy creates early demand pull (e.g., carbon pricing, renewable mandates, hydrogen pipelines), aligns asset retirements with climate pathways, and mitigates stranded‑asset risk through just‑transition and investment guarantees.

- Finance and investment scale. <cite id="25812453-0">Global energy investments must more than double to ~$5 trillion per year by 2030 (from ~$2.3 trillion today), with modeling suggesting GDP gains of ~0.4% per year due to clean energy deployment</cite>. <cite id="688848c7-1">Meeting net‑zero requires that about half of fossil fuels be equipped with carbon capture (4 Gt CO2 in 2035, 7.6 Gt in 2050), implying significant capital needs for capture and storage networks</cite>. <cite id="922c8993-3">Hydrogen supply chains and CCUS also require ~70% of 2030 electrolysis capacity and ~40% of CCUS projects already announced to meet net‑zero pathways, with the remainder dependent on policy‑driven demand and infrastructure build‑out</cite>. While financing is feasible in principle given positive expected returns and macroeconomic co‑benefits, risks include cost inflation, supply chain bottlenecks, and stranded‑portfolio concerns that raise capital costs.

- Equity, governance, and distributional feasibility. <cite id="28593032-0">Decarbonization is unevenly distributed across regions, with many fossil‑intensive economies facing lock‑in and stranded assets, underscoring that policy design, technology transfer, and finance are pivotal to equitable transitions</cite>. <cite id="fd1e4b01-3">Because most stranded‑asset risk is held by OECD investors and pension funds, global governance mechanisms must align incentives so that oil and gas phase‑out is managed to limit systemic financial shocks and support fair adjustment</cite>. <cite id="25812453-2">Developing countries can reach much of the renewable build‑out needed by 2050 under existing policies, but accelerated policy measures and stronger international support are essential to close remaining gaps</cite>.

Does environmental necessity predict global feasibility by 2050?
Taken together, the evidence supports a conditional “yes.” The climate targets set a clear direction and magnitude of change required in oil and gas use by 2050, and modeling indicates that these changes are technically achievable if deployment scales at unprecedented rates, methane is rapidly abated, and enabling infrastructure (electricity grids, hydrogen, CCUS) is built in tandem with demand‑side measures. <cite id="688848c7-0">Net‑zero by 2050 implies all fossil fuel consumption must be replaced by zero‑carbon alternatives, requiring rapid, worldwide transformation</cite> <cite id="25812453-0">IEA pathways to net zero in the energy sector show fossil fuels shrinking to ~one‑fifth of energy supply by 2050 alongside ~$5 trillion/year investments by 2030 and 8% lower total energy use by 2050</cite> <cite id="922c8993-1">Rapid methane mitigation in oil and gas alone can prevent ~0.1°C by midcentury and ~0.2°C by 2100 versus no‑action, accelerating demand reduction</cite> <cite id="25812453-4">Achieving ~50% electricity share by 2050 with 88% wind and solar implies feasible deployment trajectories if policy and supply chains enable ~390 GW/year of wind additions by 2030</cite>. However, feasibility is not guaranteed: <cite id="fd1e4b01-0">Paris‑aligned pathways imply large‑scale premature retirements of fossil plants, with gas without CCS especially vulnerable, creating stranded‑asset and reliability risks</cite> <cite id="fd1e4b01-3">Stranded asset losses could exceed $1 trillion in upstream oil and gas, concentrated in the Global North</cite> <cite id="25812453-0">Energy intensity must improve at roughly triple the historical pace to 2030, and global demand must fall despite rising activity</cite>. These constraints make feasibility contingent on governance and finance that de‑risk transitions, align asset retirements with climate targets, and mobilize capital at the necessary scale.

Practical implications for 2050
- Oil and gas supply: <cite id="922c8993-2">Full methane abatement by 2030 cuts projected warming by more than a quarter over the next decades and reduces warming by 0.1–0.5°C by 2050–2100</cite>, making supply more climate‑compatible and extending asset lives where repurposed (e.g., offshore wind/hydrogen on oil platforms). <cite id="fd1e4b01-1">Repurposing mature oil and gas platforms to renewables can extend asset lifetimes and reduce stranded costs</cite>. <cite id="922c8993-4">Even large declines in gas use can yield higher total methane emissions if abatement is insufficient, so regulatory methane caps and verification are essential</cite>.
- Renewable energy: <cite id="25812453-2">Advanced economies and China can supply most of the renewable capacity required by 2050 under existing policies, with international support critical for developing nations</cite>. <cite id="688848c7-0">Pathways converge on 70–85% renewable electricity with very low coal and near-zero gas, implying feasibility if transmission, storage, and flexibility are scaled</cite>.
- Demand‑side electrification and fuels: <cite id="25812453-3">IEA finds rapid progress in solar and BEVs and indicates ~35% fossil fuel emission cuts by 2030 are deliverable under accelerated policies</cite>. <cite id="688848c7-1">Electrification of end uses and materials/feedstock decarbonization reduce dependence on oil and gas, while CCUS covers residual emissions</cite>.

Bottom line
Environmental necessity (45% emissions cut by 2030 and net zero by 2050) predicts that global oil and gas dependence must fall dramatically by 2050, and modeling shows such global feasibility is attainable if deployment rates, methane abatement, and enabling infrastructure scale rapidly and finance and governance de‑risk transitions. <cite id="688848c7-0">Net‑zero by 2050 requires replacing fossil fuels with zero‑carbon alternatives across all sectors</cite> <cite id="25812453-0">IEA pathways show fossil shares falling to ~20% of energy by 2050 with unprecedented investment and efficiency gains</cite> <cite id="922c8993-1">Methane abatement in oil and gas yields large, low‑cost near‑term climate benefits</cite> <cite id="fd1e4b01-0">Paris‑aligned transitions imply large‑scale retirements and stranded assets, especially for gas without CCS, necessitating proactive policy design</cite> <cite id="fd1e4b01-3">Global stranded asset losses could exceed $1 trillion, concentrated among OECD investors, underscoring systemic risks and the need for coordinated transition management</cite>. The gap between what is necessary and what is predicted to be feasible narrows where methane is rapidly cut, assets are retired justly, finance is mobilized, and policies create stable demand for clean energy and hydrogen/CCUS by 2030, increasing confidence that global oil and gas dependence can be reduced in line with 2050 climate goals. </answer>

Title: Integration of energy systems
Snippet: The United Nation's dedicated body for assessing climate change, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), released the report "Global Warming of 1.5°C" to identify the risks and offer mitigation options in the face of a rapidly warming world. 6 With the exception of "overshoot" scenarios as described by the IPCC, 2050 is the definitive year in which net-zero levels of global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions must be met. Achieving net zero by 2050 implies all fossil fuel consumption needs to be replaced with or converted to zero-carbon energy alternatives. If GHG emissions continued past 2050, as in the overshoot scenarios, billions of tons of carbon dioxide would need to be removed from the atmosphere annually, using technology that has not yet been applied on a global scale.

The pathways with no overshoot or limited 1.5°C overshoot (as previously described) require a rapid, worldwide energy system transition that results in emission reductions across all sectors, including infrastructure, transportation, buildings, and industrial systems. These pathways require pronounced system changes, particularly within the next 20 years.

Other features of energy system pathways with no overshoot or limited overshoot (as previously described) include:

• Faster electrification of energy end-use • Lower energy use to meet energy service demand (through enhanced energy efficiency) • Higher share of low-emission energy sources, particularly before 2050 • Greater share (70-85%) of renewable energy-generated electricity in 2050 • Lower shares of gas-generated electricity (8%) and close to zero shares of coal-generated electricity (0-2%) • Higher shares of nuclear-and fossil fuel-generated electricity with carbon dioxide capture and storage A more recent analysis by the International Energy Agency (IEA) focused on achieving net-zero energy systems globally, and outlines fundamental transformation of global energy systems. 7 While scenarios of pathways to future net-zero energy economies are derived from a set of assumptions and limited by modeling capabilities, they serve as useful benchmarks to inform decisionmaking and, in particular, needed innovation. The IEA's path to net-zero emissions outlined is "narrow but achievable," and implies that decisions made within the next decade will have profound impact on that path's trajectory. Title: Accelerating Net Zero from the perspective of Optimizing a Carbon Capture and Utilization System
Snippet: Transition to net zero requires drastic changes across multiple energy sectors, which is difficult to realize in a short period of time. 16 From the existing to stricter schemes, the International Energy Agency (IEA) presents three scenarios 2 for the prediction of global energy transition through 2050, as shown in Fig. 1. 

Some key points are as follows: 

(1) The electricity (generation) sector produces nearly 40% of emissions in 2020 (Fig. 1b). 2 (2) The reliance on fossil fuels will decline to 67-22% in 2050 (Fig. 1c) but not disappear, because fossil fuels are required to produce carbon-embodied products (e.g., certain polymers), 2 which cannot be easily replaced by bio-materials based products. 

(3) Even if fossil fuels decline to 22%, the potential market of carbon capture is enormous, because around half of fossil fuels are required to equip with carbon capture (4 Gt CO 2 captured in 2035, while 7.6 Gt captured in 2050). 2 (4) The renewable share will grow to 25-67% in 2050 (Fig. 1d). 2 (5) Electrification will be the trend across all sectors. 2 Electricity generation will increase by 70-150% (Fig. 1e), which lays the foundation for electrification. Regarding the supply of heating utility, fossil fuels should gradually be substituted with low-carbon electricity. 2 6) A significant growth in carbon price should be introduced to regulate the GHG emissions (Fig. 1f). 2 Therefore, reducing the power plant emissions is paramount under the net-zero framework. Fossil fuels will continue to play an indispensable role through 2050, while the growth rate of renewables will be subject to a high degree of uncertainty depending on the extent of policy support. As such, there is a need for innovation that supports a stepwise transition from the current fossil-fuels based energy production to the renewable-based future. Hence, [fossil fuels + carbon capture] may be a good intermediate solution to renewables. Additionally, we can consider electrification to enhance CCU as well as the influence of carbon price.

Title: On the path to net-zero: Establishing a multi-level system to support the complex endeavor of reaching national carbon neutrality
Snippet: Furthermore, Net-Zero-2050 defined a carbon budget for Germany, which amounted to 6.9 Gt CO 2 from 2021 onward (Mengis et al., 2021). The remaining budget is estimated and provided, however, in CO 2 emissions only, based on a robust scientific basis of carbon budgets. In particular, the IPCC's remaining global CO 2 budget (after 2018) for a global mean near-surface air temperature change of 1.5 • C (relative to the 1850-1900) ranges between 420 to 840 Gt CO 2 (67 th to 33 rd percentile, respectively; Rogelj et al., 2018). Newer estimates of the remaining carbon budgets with improved uncertainty constraints amount to 315 to 755 Gt CO 2 from 2018 (Matthews et al., 2021). The Net-Zero-2050 approach for allocating a carbon budget for Germany included three phases. The first phase is the convergence phase from 2021 until 2035, where German CO 2 emissions are decreased most strongly to meet their equal-per-capita share of global emissions in 2035. As of 2035, the German share of emissions is based on Germany's equal-per-capita share of global CO 2 emissions and population projections according to the 1.5 • C scenario from the IPCC SR1.5 (Rogelj et al., 2018). In the last phase, Germany follows a net-zero CO 2 emissions trajectory after 2050 until 2100. In this project, it was also determined that CCS is assessed only in combination with carbon removal approaches. Storage of fossil-based carbon (i. e., fossil CO 2 emissions avoidance) was not considered a viable mitigation strategy due to the social acceptance of this option. In terms of mitigation deterrence, this combination could lead to postponing the end of using fossil fuels. 

The boundary conditions presented here are only valid for the research context of the Net-Zero-2050 project. Other research projects or applications in other national contexts would need to adapt the boundary conditions for their purposes in a first step.

Title: Reference forecasts for CO2 emissions from fossil-fuel combustion and cement production in Portugal
Snippet: Recently, the IPCC (2018) report has pointed that limiting global warming to 1.5 � C would require "rapid and far-reaching" transitions in land, energy, industry, buildings, transport, and cities which will require a fall of global net anthropogenic CO2 emissions by about 45% from 2010 by 2030, and reaching 'net zero' around 2050. While the IPCC report focuses on global anthropogenic emissions as the reference variable, our projections focus only on CO2 emissions from fossil fuel combustion and cement production, to which we apply literally the broader IPCC goals. As such, in this exercise we ignore any national or source-based differentiation in the international implementation of the IPCC2018 targets. 

The IPCC2018 emissions targets were applied and adopted in very general terms to the Portuguese case in the RNC2050 (2019), which establishes the strategic framework of public policies in Portugal aiming at carbon neutrality in 2050. In reality, the RNC2050 (2019) does not set specific targets for 2030 and 2050, but rather provides confidence intervals based on three alternative scenarios. Specifically, the RNC2050 (2019) points for 2030 to a range of reduction in emissions of [-45%,-55%] and to carbon neutrality by 2050 assuming a range in carbon sinks of [-85%,-90%], both relative to 2005. We apply the middle points of these ranges to the values for CO2 emissions from fossil fuels and cement production in 2005 to obtain the implicit RNC2050 targets for 2030 and 2050. Then, we change the base year from 2005 to 2010 in order to facilitate comparisons. According to these calculations, the RNC2050 targets represent a reduction of 32.2%% in emissions by 2030 while carbon neutrality by 2050 requires a reduction of 83.0%, both relative to 2010 levels. Ultimately, the RNC2050 (2019) projects a level of emissions by 2050 in line with IPCC 2018 guidelines, although by 2030 the projected reduction is slightly lower than the IPCC guidelines. 

The IPCC2018 and the RNC2050 policy targets are presented in lines 1 and 2 of Table 6.

Recently, the IPCC (2018) report has pointed that limiting global warming to 1.5 � C would require "rapid and far-reaching" transitions in land, energy, industry, buildings, transport, and cities which will require a fall of global net anthropogenic CO2 emissions by about 45% from 2010 by 2030, and reaching 'net zero' around 2050. While the IPCC report focuses on global anthropogenic emissions as the reference variable, our projections focus only on CO2 emissions from fossil fuel combustion and cement production, to which we apply literally the broader IPCC goals. As such, in this exercise we ignore any national or source-based differentiation in the international implementation of the IPCC2018 targets. 

The IPCC2018 emissions targets were applied and adopted in very general terms to the Portuguese case in the RNC2050 (2019), which establishes the strategic framework of public policies in Portugal aiming at carbon neutrality in 2050. In reality, the RNC2050 (2019) does not set specific targets for 2030 and 2050, but rather provides confidence intervals based on three alternative scenarios. Specifically, the RNC2050 (2019) points for 2030 to a range of reduction in emissions of [-45%,-55%] and to carbon neutrality by 2050 assuming a range in carbon sinks of [-85%,-90%], both relative to 2005. We apply the middle points of these ranges to the values for CO2 emissions from fossil fuels and cement production in 2005 to obtain the implicit RNC2050 targets for 2030 and 2050. Then, we change the base year from 2005 to 2010 in order to facilitate comparisons. According to these calculations, the RNC2050 targets represent a reduction of 32.2%% in emissions by 2030 while carbon neutrality by 2050 requires a reduction of 83.0%, both relative to 2010 levels. Ultimately, the RNC2050 (2019) projects a level of emissions by 2050 in line with IPCC 2018 guidelines, although by 2030 the projected reduction is slightly lower than the IPCC guidelines. 

The IPCC2018 and the RNC2050 policy targets are presented in lines 1 and 2 of Table 6.

documents.title: Integration of energy systems

The United Nation's dedicated body for assessing climate change, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), released the report "Global Warming of 1.5°C" to identify the risks and offer mitigation options in the face of a rapidly warming world. 6 With the exception of "overshoot" scenarios as described by the IPCC, 2050 is the definitive year in which net-zero levels of global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions must be met. Achieving net zero by 2050 implies all fossil fuel consumption needs to be replaced with or converted to zero-carbon energy alternatives. If GHG emissions continued past 2050, as in the overshoot scenarios, billions of tons of carbon dioxide would need to be removed from the atmosphere annually, using technology that has not yet been applied on a global scale.

The pathways with no overshoot or limited 1.5°C overshoot (as previously described) require a rapid, worldwide energy system transition that results in emission reductions across all sectors, including infrastructure, transportation, buildings, and industrial systems. These pathways require pronounced system changes, particularly within the next 20 years.

Other features of energy system pathways with no overshoot or limited overshoot (as previously described) include:

• Faster electrification of energy end-use • Lower energy use to meet energy service demand (through enhanced energy efficiency) • Higher share of low-emission energy sources, particularly before 2050 • Greater share (70-85%) of renewable energy-generated electricity in 2050 • Lower shares of gas-generated electricity (8%) and close to zero shares of coal-generated electricity (0-2%) • Higher shares of nuclear-and fossil fuel-generated electricity with carbon dioxide capture and storage A more recent analysis by the International Energy Agency (IEA) focused on achieving net-zero energy systems globally, and outlines fundamental transformation of global energy systems. 7 While scenarios of pathways to future net-zero energy economies are derived from a set of assumptions and limited by modeling capabilities, they serve as useful benchmarks to inform decisionmaking and, in particular, needed innovation. The IEA's path to net-zero emissions outlined is "narrow but achievable," and implies that decisions made within the next decade will have profound impact on that path's trajectory. documents.title: Accelerating Net Zero from the perspective of Optimizing a Carbon Capture and Utilization System
documents.snippet:
Transition to net zero requires drastic changes across multiple energy sectors, which is difficult to realize in a short period of time. 16 From the existing to stricter schemes, the International Energy Agency (IEA) presents three scenarios 2 for the prediction of global energy transition through 2050, as shown in Fig. 1. 

Some key points are as follows: 

(1) The electricity (generation) sector produces nearly 40% of emissions in 2020 (Fig. 1b). 2 (2) The reliance on fossil fuels will decline to 67-22% in 2050 (Fig. 1c) but not disappear, because fossil fuels are required to produce carbon-embodied products (e.g., certain polymers), 2 which cannot be easily replaced by bio-materials based products. 

(3) Even if fossil fuels decline to 22%, the potential market of carbon capture is enormous, because around half of fossil fuels are required to equip with carbon capture (4 Gt CO 2 captured in 2035, while 7.6 Gt captured in 2050). 2 (4) The renewable share will grow to 25-67% in 2050 (Fig. 1d). 2 (5) Electrification will be the trend across all sectors. 2 Electricity generation will increase by 70-150% (Fig. 1e), which lays the foundation for electrification. Regarding the supply of heating utility, fossil fuels should gradually be substituted with low-carbon electricity. 2 6) A significant growth in carbon price should be introduced to regulate the GHG emissions (Fig. 1f). 2 Therefore, reducing the power plant emissions is paramount under the net-zero framework. Fossil fuels will continue to play an indispensable role through 2050, while the growth rate of renewables will be subject to a high degree of uncertainty depending on the extent of policy support. As such, there is a need for innovation that supports a stepwise transition from the current fossil-fuels based energy production to the renewable-based future. Hence, [fossil fuels + carbon capture] may be a good intermediate solution to renewables. Additionally, we can consider electrification to enhance CCU as well as the influence of carbon price.

documents.snippet:
Furthermore, Net-Zero-2050 defined a carbon budget for Germany, which amounted to 6.9 Gt CO 2 from 2021 onward (Mengis et al., 2021). The remaining budget is estimated and provided, however, in CO 2 emissions only, based on a robust scientific basis of carbon budgets. In particular, the IPCC's remaining global CO 2 budget (after 2018) for a global mean near-surface air temperature change of 1.5 • C (relative to the 1850-1900) ranges between 420 to 840 Gt CO 2 (67 th to 33 rd percentile, respectively; Rogelj et al., 2018). Newer estimates of the remaining carbon budgets with improved uncertainty constraints amount to 315 to 755 Gt CO 2 from 2018 (Matthews et al., 2021). The Net-Zero-2050 approach for allocating a carbon budget for Germany included three phases. The first phase is the convergence phase from 2021 until 2035, where German CO 2 emissions are decreased most strongly to meet their equal-per-capita share of global emissions in 2035. As of 2035, the German share of emissions is based on Germany's equal-per-capita share of global CO 2 emissions and population projections according to the 1.5 • C scenario from the IPCC SR1.5 (Rogelj et al., 2018). In the last phase, Germany follows a net-zero CO 2 emissions trajectory after 2050 until 2100. In this project, it was also determined that CCS is assessed only in combination with carbon removal approaches. Storage of fossil-based carbon (i. e., fossil CO 2 emissions avoidance) was not considered a viable mitigation strategy due to the social acceptance of this option. In terms of mitigation deterrence, this combination could lead to postponing the end of using fossil fuels. 

The boundary conditions presented here are only valid for the research context of the Net-Zero-2050 project. Other research projects or applications in other national contexts would need to adapt the boundary conditions for their purposes in a first step.

This calls for drastic emission cuts up to and beyond 2050. Based on analysis presented by Rogelj et al. (2015), to achieve this goal, Rockström et al. (2017) propose a halving of gross anthropogenic CO 2 emissions every decade (from 2020) together with immediate ramping up of carbon removal to reach net-zero emissions after 2050.

This required reduction assumes: (1) a halving in global CO 2 emissions every decade from 2020 2 up to 2050 as suggested by Rockström et al. (2017); (2) emissions factors taken from the International Energy Agency (IEA, 2017a); and (3) that the ratio between coal, oil and gas is maintained at current levels (a change in ratio would only marginally change the shape of the curve).

From Figure 1, it can be concluded that, in spite of the strong growth in wind and solar since 2004 (insert plot), their shares of primary energy demand remain very low compared to fossil fuel use, and that both a highly disruptive reduction in the use of fossil fuels and increase in investments in alternatives to fossil fuels (in combinations of wind, solar, biomass, other renewables, hydro and nuclear) are required to approach near zero emissions around 2050. Title: The Role of Trade in Asia and the Pacific’s Net Zero Pathways: Overview and Policy Implications
Snippet: The International Energy Agency (IEA 2021) conducted a comprehensive study on the net zero transition for the energy sector, which accounts for three-fourths of greenhouse gases. The influential study put forward three main scenarios: (i) Stated Policy Scenario, including specific plans already in place or announced by governments; (ii) Announcement Pledges Case, where all announced national zero pledges were assumed to be achieved on time; and (iii) Net Zero Scenario by 2050, which forms the core of the analysis in the paper. The Stated Policy Scenario would lead global temperatures to rise 2.7°C, while the rise in the Pledges Case scenarios would be 2.1°C (each with a 50% probability). Net zero would be consistent with a 1.5°C rise (with a 50% probability). 

The study's net zero scenario stipulates the necessary conditions for the global energy sector to reach net zero emissions by 2050. 17 The policy challenges are daunting. The net zero pathway assumes the world economy in 2030 will be two-fifths larger than today but will use 7% less energy, requiring an energy intensity improvement of 4% per year on average to 2030, or about 3 times that achieved over the past 2 decades. It will require a major increase in renewable energy use, energy efficiency, and clean energy innovations, while fossil fuels will have to shrink to about one-fifth of the energy supply by 2050, from about four-fifths today. Moreover, the net zero scenario requires that global energy demand by 2050 fall by 8%, posing a considerable challenge with 2 billion additional people on the planet. Emissions from industry, transport, and buildings will have to fall by 95% by 2050, requiring major efforts to build new and retool existing infrastructure. 

Investments associated with the shift toward net zero are massive. 

The IEA study uses modeling undertaken with the International Monetary Fund to calculate annual investment requirements for the energy sector. It concludes that such investments will need to more than double to $5 trillion by 2030, from about $2.3 trillion currently. On the positive side, this should add 0.4% to annual global GDP growth.

Title: An Optimization Approaches and Control Strategies of Hydrogen Fuel Cell Systems in EDG-Integration Based on DVR Technology
Snippet: Tripling the capacity of renewable energy sources constitutes the primary mechanism for achieving emission reductions by 2030 within the context of the Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario. Advanced economies and China are anticipated to attain approximately 85% of the requisite renewable capacity by the year 2030 under existing policy frameworks. However, to realize similar advancements in other developing nations, the implementation of more vigorous policy measures and enhanced international support are imperative. This strategic expansion is essential for aligning global energy practices with the ambitious targets set forth in the NZE Scenario, highlighting a pivotal shift towards sustainable energy systems. Following this, reducing methane emissions from the energy sector yields substantial climate advantages. Within the frame-work of the Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario, it is estimated that approximately USD 75 billion in cumulative investment is needed by 2030 to implement all methane abatement strategies in the oil and gas industry. Remarkably, this investment represents merely 2% of the net income that the oil and gas sector recorded in 2022. This juxtaposition underscores the economic feasibility of significant methane reduction measures relative to the industry's financial capabilities, highlighting an efficient pathway towards mitigating one of the most potent greenhouse gases [76][77][78][79][80]. 

Emerging technologies like hydrogen and carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) are projected to play a pivotal role in emissions reduction primarily post-2030. In the context of the Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario (NZE Scenario), if all currently announced projects for hydrogen electrolysis capacity come to fruition, they are anticipated to fulfil approximately 70% of the requisite capacity by 2030. Similarly, the CCUS projects that have been announced, predominantly within advanced economies, are expected to meet nearly 40% of the global requirements by the same year. These figures underscore a critical need for enhanced policy measures aimed at fostering demand for low-emission products and fuels, thereby ensuring these technologies achieve their potential in reducing greenhouse gas emissions effectively and sustainably. In this direction, the realization of hydrogen deployment as outlined in the Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario (NZE Scenario) hinges critically on significant investments in the production, transmission, and distribution of low-emissions hydrogen and hydrogen-based fuels.

Under the IEA Stated Policies (STEPS) scenario, offshore wind IC increases to about 180 GW in 2030, and 380 GW by 2050, while the IEA Sustainable Development Scenario (SDS) increases offshore wind IC to 220 GW in 2030 and 590 GW by 2050 [31]. Under this ambitious scenario, annual wind energy IC additions reach 390 GW/y by 2030 (from 114 GW/y in 2020), leading to around 8000 GW wind IC by 2050 [14] (Figures 3 and 4). Tripling the capacity of renewable energy sources constitutes the primary mechanism for achieving emission reductions by 2030 within the context of the Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario. Advanced economies and China are anticipated to attain approximately 85% of the requisite renewable capacity by the year 2030 under existing policy frameworks. However, to realize similar advancements in other developing nations, the implementation of more vigorous policy measures and enhanced international support are imperative. This strategic expansion is essential for aligning global energy practices with the ambitious targets set forth in the NZE Scenario, highlighting a pivotal shift towards sustainable energy systems. Following this, reducing methane emissions from the energy sector yields substantial climate advantages. Within the frame-work of the Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario, it is estimated that approximately USD 75 billion in cumulative investment is needed by 2030 to implement all methane abatement strategies in the oil and gas industry. Remarkably, this investment represents merely 2% of the net income that the oil and gas sector recorded in 2022. This juxtaposition underscores the economic feasibility of significant methane reduction measures relative to the industry's financial capabilities, highlighting an efficient pathway towards mitigating one of the most potent greenhouse gases [76][77][78][79][80]. 

Emerging technologies like hydrogen and carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) are projected to play a pivotal role in emissions reduction primarily post-2030. In the context of the Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario (NZE Scenario), if all currently announced projects for hydrogen electrolysis capacity come to fruition, they are anticipated to fulfil approximately 70% of the requisite capacity by 2030. Similarly, the CCUS projects that have been announced, predominantly within advanced economies, are expected to meet nearly 40% of the global requirements by the same year. These figures underscore a critical need for enhanced policy measures aimed at fostering demand for low-emission products and fuels, thereby ensuring these technologies achieve their potential in reducing greenhouse gas emissions effectively and sustainably. In this direction, the realization of hydrogen deployment as outlined in the Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario (NZE Scenario) hinges critically on significant investments in the production, transmission, and distribution of low-emissions hydrogen and hydrogen-based fuels.

Title: Is hydrogen production through natural gas pyrolysis compatible with ambitious climate targets in the United States? A location-specific, time-resolved analysis
Snippet: Three scenarios for methane emission mitigation along the natural gas supply chain were considered. 

In the first, most conservative scenario 'current regulations' , only the effect of state regulations (+ Canada), where an estimate of or target for the regulations' effect on methane emissions has been provided (CA, CO, NM, PA, Canada, see table 1) is considered. In this scenario, year-by-year basinspecific emission factor decreases as a consequence of state regulation are calculated. Then, the effect of basin-specific emission factors on state-specific, consumption-normalized emission factors are traced based on the natural gas flow analysis provided by Burns and Grubert (Burns and Grubert 2021a). 

In the second scenario, 'EPA rule' , the effect of a proposed federal EPA rule (RIN: 2060-AV16) on CH 4 emissions nationwide based on the EPA Regulatory Impact Assessment (incl. Canadian regulation) is considered. 

In the third, most ambitious scenario 'rapid action' , it is assumed that, starting from 2023, the CH 4 emission factors are linearly reduced until 2030 to 31% of the current emission factors and then remain constant until 2050. This corresponds to the abatement potential of 69% that has been identified by the IEA for US natural gas production (IEA 2021b). The target date for mitigation until 2030 is in agreement with the Global Methane Pledge. Other researchers have used more ambitious goals of 77%-83% global abatement, which include company commitments based on Oil and Gas Climate Initiative (OGCI) goals; however, OGCI members produce only a small fraction of US natural gas (Ocko et al 2021). 

For methane emissions from coal mining, a 45% linear reduction in the methane intensity of coal supply from 2023 to 2030 is applied across all three scenarios (IEA 2021a). It should be noted that methane emissions from coal mining contribute little to temperature changes in 2050 in these calculations because of the rapid phase-out of coal in the net-zero-by-2050 scenarios.

Title: Acting rapidly to deploy readily available methane mitigation measures by sector can immediately slow global warming
Snippet: The majority of economically feasible actions come from the oil and gas sector, accounting for around 80% of the avoided warming from economically feasible methane mitigation actions over all timescales (figure 4); 20% of this avoided warming comes from agreed upon targets by top oil and gas companies to reduce upstream leakage (OGCI 2018). We find that implementing current net zero cost oil and gas supply chain mitigation measures, such as leak detection and repair programs, along with fulfilment of company commitments of capped leakage rates, could avoid around 0.1 • C of global-mean warming by midcentury and 0.2 • C by end of century relative to a no further action baseline that suggests the oil and gas sector could contribute 0.15 • C to warming by 2050 and 0.25 • C by 2100 (figure 4). 

For technically feasible mitigation, abatement measures for landfills and livestock play important roles in addition to oil and gas (figure 4). Implementation of all available landfill measures (requiring at most only minor improvements)-such as source separation-could avoid 0.16 • C of globalmean warming in 2100 relative to a no further action baseline (figure 4). Deploying all livestock abatement strategies-such as methane inhibitors and improved manure management-could avoid nearly 0.1 • C of global-mean warming in 2100 relative to a no further action baseline (figure 4). However, given the amount of livestock emissions that currently cannot be addressed with existing technologies, residual methane emissions from livestock are expected to contribute to half of the remaining future methane emissions unless there are behavioral changes and technological advancements. 

Given that there are specific uncertainties associated with methane's climate impacts in addition to the various uncertainties associated with all models and emissions estimates, we perform several sensitivity tests to assess how methane-related model parameters affect our results. For example, there are uncertainties associated with the radiative effects from methane's oxidation processes and methane's atmospheric lifetime. Overall, the consideration of their individual uncertainties in our analysis suggests a global-mean temperature rise by end of century from baseline methane emissions that ranges from 0.75 • C to 1.5 • C; see supplementary material for more details.

Title: Acting rapidly to deploy readily available methane mitigation measures by sector can immediately slow global warming
Snippet: The goal of this study is to assess the value of rapidly deploying available methane mitigation measures as compared to slower implementation timelines or delayed action, with an emphasis on sectoral contributions to climate benefits over all timescales. We find that while the potential to reduce methane emissions  C by sector for methane mitigation measures fully employed by 2030 and maintained throughout the 21st century, for both economically and technically feasible measures. Economically feasible measures ('econ') refer to current no net cost options. For oil and gas, we include commitments made by oil and gas companies, with the assumption that companies have found it fits into their business models. The contribution of company commitments to avoided warming beyond current no net cost options is shown in the line pattern ('econ cc'). Technically feasible measures include all readily available technologies in addition to no net cost options. Note that the sum of sector totals are slightly than those in figure 3 with existing mitigation measures varies considerably by sector, if deployed in parallel can cut expected 2030 methane emissions in half, with a quarter at no net cost. We find that full deployment of these available mitigation measures by 2030 can slow the rate of global-mean warming over the next few decades by more than 25%, while preventing around a quarter degree ( • C) of additional global-mean warming in 2050 and half a degree ( • C) in 2100. On the other hand, slow or delayed methane action leads to a 5% or nearly 20% increase in global-mean warming rate from 2030 to 2050 relative to fast action, respectively. Oil and gas measures dominate the avoided warming from economically feasible actions, and landfill measures play a secondary role to oil and gas in the avoided warming from technically feasible actions. Livestock measures also play an important role for technically feasible methane mitigation, but a considerable fraction of emissions from livestock still remain unabated.

Snippet: All scenarios lead to net-zero emissions for the combined methane and CO 2 emissions (Fig. 4). Tripling the capacity of renewable energy sources constitutes the primary mechanism for achieving emission reductions by 2030 within the context of the Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario. Advanced economies and China are anticipated to attain approximately 85% of the requisite renewable capacity by the year 2030 under existing policy frameworks. However, to realize similar advancements in other developing nations, the implementation of more vigorous policy measures and enhanced international support are imperative. This strategic expansion is essential for aligning global energy practices with the ambitious targets set forth in the NZE Scenario, highlighting a pivotal shift towards sustainable energy systems. Following this, reducing methane emissions from the energy sector yields substantial climate advantages. Within the frame-work of the Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario, it is estimated that approximately USD 75 billion in cumulative investment is needed by 2030 to implement all methane abatement strategies in the oil and gas industry. Remarkably, this investment represents merely 2% of the net income that the oil and gas sector recorded in 2022. This juxtaposition underscores the economic feasibility of significant methane reduction measures relative to the industry's financial capabilities, highlighting an efficient pathway towards mitigating one of the most potent greenhouse gases [76][77][78][79][80]. 

Emerging technologies like hydrogen and carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) are projected to play a pivotal role in emissions reduction primarily post-2030. In the context of the Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario (NZE Scenario), if all currently announced projects for hydrogen electrolysis capacity come to fruition, they are anticipated to fulfil approximately 70% of the requisite capacity by 2030. Similarly, the CCUS projects that have been announced, predominantly within advanced economies, are expected to meet nearly 40% of the global requirements by the same year. These figures underscore a critical need for enhanced policy measures aimed at fostering demand for low-emission products and fuels, thereby ensuring these technologies achieve their potential in reducing greenhouse gas emissions effectively and sustainably. In this direction, the realization of hydrogen deployment as outlined in the Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario (NZE Scenario) hinges critically on significant investments in the production, transmission, and distribution of low-emissions hydrogen and hydrogen-based fuels.

documents.snippet: All scenarios lead to net-zero emissions for the combined methane and CO 2 emissions (Fig. 4). However, the distribution between methane and CO 2 emissions varies, especially for 2030 and 2040. While methane emissions in 2030 follow the expected trend with the BAT scenario having the lowest methane emissions, followed by the HP and CEF scenarios, the differences in methane emissions in 2040 narrow down and methane emissions of HP exceed CEF in 2050. The change of position between the HP and CEF scenarios in 2050 is due to the significant reduction in natural gas use in the CEF scenario in 2050, corresponding to 50% of the natural gas used in the HP scenario. Yet, both the HP and CEF scenarios have significantly larger methane emissions despite the lower natural gas primary energy demand, highlighting the importance of methane emissions' abatement. Net removal of CO 2 from the atmosphere is required in 2050 in all scenarios to offset unabated methane emissions along the natural gas value chain. HP and CEF require 50% and 15% more net CO 2 removal than the BAT scenario. Removal is achieved through a combination of bioenergy with CCS (BECCS) in the power, industry and hydrogen production sectors and direct air carbon capture and storage (DACCS).

Title: Stranded asset implications of the Paris Agreement in Latin America and the Caribbean
Snippet: The four mitigation scenarios are characterized by a major transformation of the energy system by 2050 (supplementary figure 3), including increased energy efficiency and conservation, a transition from emitting fossil-fuel technologies (such as oil and gas power and petroleum based transportation) to low-and noncarbon emitting technologies (including renewable electricity, carbon capture and sequestration, and liquid biofuels), and a shift in the type of investments throughout the energy system. 

Here, we focus on stranded assets and investments in the power sector, an important sector in the context of climate change mitigation [4], as a conservative measure of the scale and value of stranded assets in LAC. Across the mitigation scenarios explored in this study, between 60 GW (Straight-to-2 °C) and 128 GW (NDCs-to-1.5 °C) of fossil-fuel power plants are prematurely retired before the end of their physical lifetimes in the LAC power sector from 2021 to 2050 (figure 2; supplementary table 5). These amounts are equivalent to 15%-33% of the total installed capacity in 2015 in LAC (approximately 393 GW) [51]. Since the NDCs-to-1.5 °C scenario requires the fastest reductions in CO 2 emissions, the magnitude of stranded assets in that scenario is also greatest, resulting in nearly 50% more stranding than the Straight-to-1.5 

°C scenario and more than double the stranded capacity observed in the Straight-to-2 °C scenario. Most of this stranding occurs between 2031 and 2035, when LAC energy and industry emissions are reduced by nearly 75%. Over 80 GW of capacity is prematurely retired over this five-year period. Natural gas and oil power plants without carbon capture and sequestration storage (CCS) represent the largest fraction of prematurely retired capacity in our scenarios in LAC. In our scenarios, natural gas without CCS accounts for about 45% of stranded capacity in the NDCs-to-2 °C scenario and about 54% of stranded capacity in the NDCs-to-1.5 °C scenario, calling to question natural gas's role as a 'bridge fuel' [52].

Title: Synergies in offshore energy: a roadmap for the Danish sector
Snippet: The Oil & Gas (O&G) sector is facing many challenges. These include international climate frameworks such as the Paris Agreement, consistently low crude oil prices together and the foreseeable End Of Life (EOL) of many O&G assets. On the one hand, there is need to clarify the implications of the wider energy transition on existing O&G operations. On the other hand, much offshore infrastructure is reaching or will soon reach (e.g. within 30 years) the end of its economically operational lifetime. The decision of the Danish Government in December 2020 to cancel new O&G explorations in the Danish North Sea means all existing production must have ceased by 2050. Faced with potentially very high decommissioning costs for this infrastructure, the O&G sector may benefit from a partial or complete repurposing of this infrastructure, during and/or after its operational lifetime. This report presents the findings of a feasibility study about exploiting synergies between offshore O&G and renewable energy activities in the Danish Underground Consortium (DUC) region of the North Sea. The objective was to develop a roadmap for this sector out to 2050. The project was funded by the DHRTC alongside six other projects exploring the technical and economic feasibility of alternative uses for existing O&G infrastructure. The research was carried out from September 2020 to January 2021 between the School of Engineering, University of Aberdeen, and the Division of Sustainability, DTU Management, Technical University of Denmark. The very short timeframe and small project team mean that the analysis is relatively high-level, requiring many simplifying assumptions and resulting in some important technical details being overlooked and left for future research. For this reason, this report should be understood as a starting point for further and more detailed analysis, rather than a definitive roadmap for the sector.

This study consists of two main parts. The first performs a techno-economic analysis and screening of relevant coupling technologies between the two sectors, including offshore wind, hydrogen production with electrolysis and carbon capture and storage (CCS). Title: Trump’s “America first” energy policy, contingency and the reconfiguration of the global energy order
Snippet: The global fossil fuel system, according to IRENA (2019, 64), relies on a massive built-in infrastructure of oil wells, pipelines, tankers and refineries. This stock of physical assets worth US $25 trillion may be stranded due to technological innovations and government efforts to switch to renewables and low-carbon alternatives. Van de Graaf and Bradshaw (2018) predict that the established oil producers might "end up with lower future revenues from [their] assets (the bursting of the 'carbon bubble'), capital investments in oil infrastructure that cannot be recovered because of reduced demand or reduced prices ('stranded assets') and existing oil reserves that are left unexploited ('unburnable oil reserves')" (1322). On the other hand, the interlocking web of infrastructure, technologies and institutions underpinning the existing fossil fuel-based system creates a path-dependent process of 'carbon lock-in' which inhibits transitions toward low-carbon alternatives (Seto et al., 2016). 

According to available geological estimates, there are large reserves of recoverable shale oil and gas in the United States, Canada and worldwide. Global estimates for shale oil are 345 billion barrels (Bbbl) and for shale gas are at least 100 trillion cubic ft 3 (Tcf); estimates for US recoverable shale oil are 58 Bbbl and estimated shale gas reserves are 600-1000 Tcf (Jackson et al., 2014, 329). 

Given the 345 Bbbl shale-oil reserves at the price of oil US$100/ barrel, shale-oil reserves are worth US$35 trillion (Jackson et al., 2014, 329). For comparison, sovereign wealth funds (SWFs) held $7.45 trillion in total assets (as of March 2018). Norway's Pension Fund Global with US$1.06 trillion is the world's largest SFW followed by China Investment Corporation, Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and Kuwait Investment Authority (Milhench, 2018). 

The shale boom during the recent commodity super-cycle led to the renewal of US oil production where output rose from 5 million bbd in 2008 to an average of more than 8.5 million b/d in 2014 and now stands F. Guliyev at about 10 million bbd.

Title: Stranded fossil-fuel assets translate to major losses for investors in advanced economies
Snippet: The distribution of ownership of transition risk associated with stranded fossil-fuel assets remains poorly understood. We calculate that global stranded assets as present value of future lost profits in the upstream oil and gas sector exceed US$1 trillion under plausible changes in expectations about the effects of climate policy. We trace the equity risk ownership from 43,439 oil and gas production assets through a global equity network of 1.8 million companies to their ultimate owners. Most of the market risk falls on private investors, overwhelmingly in OECD countries, including substantial exposure through pension funds and financial markets. The ownership distribution reveals an international net transfer of more than 15% of global stranded asset risk to OECD-based investors. Rich country stakeholders therefore have a major stake in how the transition in oil and gas production is managed, as ongoing supporters of the fossil-fuel economy and potentially exposed owners of stranded assets. The necessary and rapid transition to a low-carbon economy will lead to massive stranded assets, which could risk the stability of financial markets and the economy. Through a global equity network, most risk and responsibility is owned by investors, such as pension funds, in developed countries.

Title: Ten new insights in climate science 2023
Snippet: Furthermore, they create 'carbon lock-in': it is harder to stop fossil fuel projects from operating once they are built, since companies tend to pursue full-lifetime use of assets to recover sunk investment. Yet, governments and companies still plan on extracting vastly more fossil fuels than is consistent with the 1.5°C warming limit target, thereby creating a so-called 'production gap' (Rekker et al., 2023;SEI et al., 2023). Government subsidies for fossil fuel production and use also reached an all-time high of 1 trillion USD in 2022 (IEA, 2023b). 

Fossil fuel expansion is also perpetuated by financial actors through their investments and company ownership. Potential economic losses from stranded assets in upstream oil and gas are estimated upward of 1 trillion USD, held predominantly in the Global North through cross-border financial stakes in oil and gas fields elsewhere (Semieniuk et al., 2022). Stranded assets can have macroeconomic consequences by affecting the valuation of other assets, that is, contagion and triggering spillovers from the financial to the real economy (Campiglio & van der Ploeg,  (Tong et al., 2019) and of fossil fuel extracting infrastructure (Trout et al, 2022), also showing proposed 'carbon bombs', defined as fossil fuel extraction projects whose lifetime emissions exceed 1 Gt CO 2 (Kühne et al, 2022). These are compared with the remaining carbon budget (Friedlingstein et al., 2022) updated for early 2023 (Forster et al., 2023). While the estimates for existing infrastructure are comprehensive, those for proposed infrastructure are partial due to lack of available data on consuming infrastructure in industry, transport, buildings, or other, or on smaller future extraction projects. 'Existing' generally means that capital has been invested or committed, as at the start of 2018 (see original papers for further details on methods). New infrastructure built since then will likely exceed retirements and reductions in remaining life, hence an updated estimate would likely be larger. Since the infrastructure estimates for extraction and consumption relate to different ends of the supply chain, they are non-additive: each carbon atom passes through both extraction and combustion stages.

attempts.answer:
Summary
Reducing global reliance on oil and gas is an environmental necessity for a sustainable, livable climate and cleaner air, and the transition is already underway in power and transport even as corporate and investment behavior lags climate‑compliant trajectories. IPCC and IEA analyses of 1.5°C–2°C‑consistent pathways show oil, gas, and coal use must fall by several-fold by mid‑century, whereas “business‑as‑usual” policies increase the fossil share of energy and lock in incompatible warming. Health evidence ties fossil fuel combustion to fine particulate matter (PM2.5), ozone, and millions of premature deaths annually, reinforcing that decarbonization is a public health imperative. On the demand side, renewables reached 30% of global electricity in 2023 with record additions, EV stocks surpassed 40 million by late 2023, and policy toolkits (carbon pricing, renewable mandates, EV incentives) are expanding. On the supply side, IEA and allied analyses show oil and gas demand rose recently, corporate portfolios still over‑allocate to fossil fuels, and methane/CO2 intensity pressures are altering trade and investment. The combined picture is progress plus a significant unfinished agenda.

Why reducing oil and gas is an environmental necessity
- Climate science requires deep fossil fuel phase‑down. Pathways that limit warming to 1.5°C or well below 2°C require steep declines in fossil energy use by around 2050, with many integrated assessment models projecting near‑zero shares of coal and very low shares of unabated gas, and most residual fossil use offset by CO2 capture or non‑fossil renewables. <cite id="094fce18-3">Achieving net zero by 2050 implies all fossil fuel consumption needs to be replaced with or converted to zero-carbon energy alternatives; across no‑overshoot pathways there is a rapid shift to higher shares of renewables and near zero coal by 2050</cite>. <cite id="094fce18-0">Across IEA scenarios, coal and oil decline by roughly 75–90% and gas by roughly 55% by 2050 in the Net Zero Emissions (NZE) case, whereas many pathways for 1.5°C imply gas declines of roughly 45% by 2050</cite>. <cite id="094fce18-1">In the IEA ensemble, scenarios consistent with announced policies (APS) or stricter SDS/NZE cut the fossil share of total energy to 53, 36, and 22% by 2050, respectively, versus increases to 66% under a STEPS “fossil‑heavy” baseline; NZE/SDS require large reductions in fossil fuels</cite>.
- Fossil fuel use is incompatible with climate and health targets at current scales. <cite id="094fce18-4">IPCC‑aligned net‑zero systems require significant reduction in overall fossil fuel consumption with minimal use of unabated fossil fuels, and IEA asserts net‑zero by 2050 requires timely phasing out of oil and gas</cite>. <cite id="304f1489-0">Fossil fuels are a major source of PM2.5 and ozone; in 2019, PM2.5 and O3 were linked to 6.7 million deaths, with fossil fuels associated with 61% of PM2.5/O3 mortality globally in 2019</cite>. <cite id="304f1489-3">Fossil fuel combustion is responsible for most U.S. GHGs and a majority of PM2.5‑related premature mortality, and climate mitigation policies can deliver co‑benefits for air quality and public health</cite>.
- Sectoral evidence links combustion to harms and co‑benefits from decarbonization. <cite id="304f1489-1">Electricity generating units and residential/commercial combustion contribute large shares of PM2.5‑ and ozone‑related premature mortality in the United States</cite>. <cite id="304f1489-2">In Poland, over half of PM2.5 and PM10 emissions originate from coal and wood combustion, driving elevated local health burdens</cite>. <cite id="304f1489-3">Emissions from power plants, roads, and industrial facilities disproportionately affect communities of color, evidencing environmental injustice alongside climate risk</cite>.

Is the reduction occurring?
- Power sector decarbonization at record pace. <cite id="004e29c0-2">Renewables reached 30% of global electricity generation in 2023; 2024 saw 585 GW of new renewable capacity with 92.5% of expansion being renewables and a record 15.1% annual growth</cite>. <cite id="004e29c0-2">Wind and solar tripled and seven‑folded global electricity generation, respectively, from 2014 to 2022; by 2028, renewables could supply 42% of global generation under IEA projections</cite>. <cite id="004e29c0-2">China supplies over 40% of global solar PV and onshore wind capacity and more than half of offshore wind, underscoring market concentration in leading decarbonizers</cite>.
- Transport electrification is accelerating. <cite id="004e29c0-0">In 2023, 14 million new electric cars were registered worldwide, bringing total EV stock to ~40 million; China overtook Europe as the top sales market in 2021 and maintained a lead through 2024</cite>. <cite id="004e29c0-3">Global EV sales reached ~14 million in 2023 (about 18% of total), with the U.S. targeting 500,000 public chargers by 2030</cite>. <cite id="004e29c0-4">Solar accounted for over 50% of renewable additions from 2019–2021 and is projected to be ~60% of 2022 additions, enabled by falling costs (Lazard: wind 2–6 cents/kWh; solar ~3–7 cents/kWh) and supportive policies</cite>.
- Policy toolkits and market signals are expanding. <cite id="004e29c0-3">Since 2019, many countries have strengthened energy transition policies—fiscal incentives, renewable portfolio standards, emissions trading systems, and grid/EV charging investments—shifting capital toward low‑carbon projects, changing the power mix, and lowering wholesale electricity prices and volatility in 2024</cite>. <cite id="68bfda25-0">EU policy is embedding carbon intensity in trade and pricing: the carbon border adjustment mechanism levies on gas imports that do not meet EU carbon‑intensity standards, and some trading platforms already price crude by carbon intensity, increasing competitiveness penalties for high‑emitting “legacy” supplies</cite>. <cite id="094fce18-4">Legal and policy frameworks increasingly frame a “phase out” of fossil fuels as necessary to meet climate goals, coordinating supply‑side limits on extraction and demand‑side actions to curb consumption</cite>.
- Corporate and investment patterns show both movement and misalignment. <cite id="68bfda25-0">Higher oil and gas prices since 2022 boosted upstream capex by 12% in 2023, but most new investment is flowing to “advantaged barrel” basins with lower emissions and fast delivery; supermajors and explorers are reassessing portfolios under net‑zero targets</cite>. <cite id="68bfda25-1">The global energy crisis and geopolitical shifts have reshaped supply‑demand patterns since Russia‑Ukraine war, with Europe and Asia‑Pacific facing large supply gaps and relying on resource‑rich regions in “four circles and two systems” trade pattern</cite>. <cite id="68bfda25-4">As of March 2024, the strategies of the world’s 114 largest oil and gas companies are on track to exceed their 1.5°C‑compatible share of future GHG emissions by 59% in 2030 and 189% in 2040 (up from 43% and 120% in 2016); 33 companies exceed 300% of a 1.5°C‑compatible share by 2040, and eight of the nine largest are national oil companies projected to supply 30% of global production in 2040 while over‑shooting by 226%</cite>. <cite id="68bfda25-3">IEA demand scenarios note oil demand may rise to 105.7 mb/d by 2028 before growth slows, with EVs/biofuels potentially peaking demand; carbon intensity targets for oil and gas may reduce emissions per barrel but not total emissions without absolute production reductions</cite>.
- Co‑benefits and equity are materializing and highlighted. <cite id="304f1489-3">Because fossil plants emit both GHGs and health‑damaging pollutants, climate mitigation delivers co‑benefits in improved air quality; however, burdens are unequally distributed, with communities near power plants and major roads experiencing disproportionate PM2.5 exposure and mortality</cite>. <cite id="304f1489-2">Household reliance on coal and wood in some countries like Poland amplifies local PM2.5, with Europe reporting ~307,000 premature deaths in 2019 alone from PM2.5 and 40,400 from NO2</cite>.

Where progress is lagging and why it remains insufficient
- Fossil demand is still rising in the short run, and corporate strategies remain misaligned with 1.5°C. <cite id="68bfda25-4">Despite policy signals and recent cost declines, the aggregate strategies of major oil and gas firms imply overshooting 1.5°C‑compatible emission shares by wide margins in 2030 and 2040</cite>. <cite id="68bfda25-0">Upstream investment rebounds to ~12% higher in 2023 and prioritizes advantaged basins, while trading and border measures penalize higher‑intensity supplies; nonetheless, entry barriers and legacy assets keep the industry’s footprint large</cite>.
- Baselines differ across scenarios; without stronger near‑term policies, fossil shares can increase. <cite id="094fce18-1">Under the IEA STEPS “fossil‑heavy” path, fossil fuels rise to 66% of total primary energy by 2050 versus declines to 53, 36, and 22% under APS, SDS, and NZE, respectively</cite>. <cite id="094fce18-2">AR6‑consistent ensembles project median +37% increase in natural gas demand to 2050 with large uncertainty ranges, underscoring that even “bridge” uses of gas may not be compatible with 1.5°C unless paired with CCS and broader electrification</cite>.
- Health and climate risks remain acute. <cite id="304f1489-0">Global PM2.5 and ozone mortality remains in the millions, with a large share attributable to fossil combustion; phasing out fossil fuels could avert millions of premature deaths</cite>. <cite id="304f1489-3">In the U.S., half of PM2.5‑related premature deaths are attributable to fossil fuels, and exposure disparities fall disproportionately on communities of color</cite>.

What would accelerate and deepen the shift
- Strengthen near‑term policy ambition and coverage. <cite id="094fce18-4">Combining supply‑side limits on extraction with demand‑side reductions is the core legal and practical framework for phasing out fossil fuels, with “no new exploration/production” pledges and managed declines of existing assets</cite>. <cite id="68bfda25-0">Carbon border/climate‑intensity standards in trade and pricing are already reshaping competitiveness for high‑emitting fossil supplies and can be deepened to require near‑zero emissions in traded fuels</cite>.
- Mobilize finance toward clean energy and away from fossil. <cite id="004e29c0-2">Record renewable additions and falling Lazard levelized costs (wind 2–6 cents/kWh; solar ~3–7 cents/kWh) make deployment bankable, but public and private capital still favors advantaged fossil assets</cite>. <cite id="68bfda25-0">Directing upstream capex to advantaged, lower‑emitting basins while halting new legacy “super‑emitter” projects and flaring would narrow carbon intensity, though absolute production must fall to meet 1.5°C</cite>.
- Prioritize health and equity co‑benefits. <cite id="304f1489-3">Air‑quality improvements from decarbonization and local clean‑heat transitions yield immediate health gains and reduce environmental inequities</cite>. <cite id="304f1489-2">Reducing reliance on coal and wood in households can deliver large local PM2.5 reductions where burdens are highest</cite>.

Bottom line
- Necessity: The physics of climate and the epidemiology of air pollution establish that reducing oil and gas dependence is essential to limit warming and avert catastrophic health outcomes; credible 1.5°C/2°C pathways require multi‑fold declines in fossil fuel use by mid‑century. <cite id="094fce18-3">Net‑zero by 2050 requires replacing fossil consumption with zero‑carbon alternatives and rapidly scaling renewables and electrification</cite> <cite id="094fce18-0">IEA NZE projects oil and gas declines of roughly 55–78% by 2050</cite> <cite id="094fce18-1">SDS/NZE cut fossil shares of total energy to 22–36% by 2050 versus increases under STEPS</cite> <cite id="304f1489-0">Fossil fuels are linked to ~6–8 million premature deaths in 2019–2023 estimates, with a large share attributable to combustion</cite>.
- Occurrence: The shift is real and accelerating in the power and transport sectors, with renewables at ~30% of global electricity in 2023, record clean energy additions, and EV stocks surpassing 40 million, supported by expanding policy frameworks and market signals. <cite id="004e29c0-2">Renewables reached 30% of electricity in 2023, with 585 GW of new capacity and 15.1% growth in 2024</cite> <cite id="004e29c0-0">EV registrations reached 14 million in 2023, with China leading global sales</cite> <cite id="004e29c0-3">Policies on carbon pricing, RPS, and EV incentives are expanding and already changing power mixes and infrastructure</cite>.
- Gaps: Despite these gains, oil and gas demand rose recently, corporate strategies and investment remain over‑aligned with fossil overuse, and many pathways without stronger near‑term policies still lock in incompatible warming. <cite id="68bfda25-4">Major oil and gas companies’ strategies imply overshooting 1.5°C‑compatible emission shares by large margins in 2030 and 2040</cite> <cite id="094fce18-1">Fossil shares can rise to 66% under fossil‑heavy baselines absent stricter policies</cite>.

What this means for a sustainable future
- To achieve environmental sustainability, countries must translate current momentum into stronger, binding 2030 milestones that cut oil and gas use in line with 1.5°C‑consistent pathways, while accelerating clean energy deployment and transport electrification. <cite id="094fce18-4">Supply‑side restrictions on fossil extraction combined with demand‑side action are the legal and practical core of phase‑out</cite> <cite id="094fce18-3">Pathways converge on 70–85% renewable electricity by 2050 with near‑zero coal and very limited unabated gas, implying deep phase‑down of oil and gas across sectors</cite>. The next decade of decisions—investment direction, carbon pricing/standards, and fossil leasing—will determine whether the world finishes the transition in time or compounds the costs of inaction. <cite id="094fce18-3">Per IEA analysis, decisions made within the next decade have profound impacts on the trajectory of net‑zero pathways</cite>.

Snippet: The United Nation's dedicated body for assessing climate change, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), released the report "Global Warming of 1.5°C" to identify the risks and offer mitigation options in the face of a rapidly warming world. 6 With the exception of "overshoot" scenarios as described by the IPCC, 2050 is the definitive year in which net-zero levels of global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions must be met. Achieving net zero by 2050 implies all fossil fuel consumption needs to be replaced with or converted to zero-carbon energy alternatives. If GHG emissions continued past 2050, as in the overshoot scenarios, billions of tons of carbon dioxide would need to be removed from the atmosphere annually, using technology that has not yet been applied on a global scale.

The pathways with no overshoot or limited 1.5°C overshoot (as previously described) require a rapid, worldwide energy system transition that results in emission reductions across all sectors, including infrastructure, transportation, buildings, and industrial systems. These pathways require pronounced system changes, particularly within the next 20 years.

Other features of energy system pathways with no overshoot or limited overshoot (as previously described) include:

• Faster electrification of energy end-use • Lower energy use to meet energy service demand (through enhanced energy efficiency) • Higher share of low-emission energy sources, particularly before 2050 • Greater share (70-85%) of renewable energy-generated electricity in 2050 • Lower shares of gas-generated electricity (8%) and close to zero shares of coal-generated electricity (0-2%) • Higher shares of nuclear-and fossil fuel-generated electricity with carbon dioxide capture and storage A more recent analysis by the International Energy Agency (IEA) focused on achieving net-zero energy systems globally, and outlines fundamental transformation of global energy systems. 7 While scenarios of pathways to future net-zero energy economies are derived from a set of assumptions and limited by modeling capabilities, they serve as useful benchmarks to inform decisionmaking and, in particular, needed innovation. The IEA's path to net-zero emissions outlined is "narrow but achievable," and implies that decisions made within the next decade will have profound impact on that path's trajectory. Title: The challenge of phasing out fossil fuels for highly fossil fuel-dependent countries in international law
Snippet: In contrast to renewable resources, fossil fuels, including oil, natural gas, and coal, are nonrenewable resources whose combustion produces large amounts of energy and CO2. According to the sixth report of the IPCC, Net-Zero CO2 energy systems require a significant reduction in overall fossil fuel consumption and minimal use of unabated fossil fuels. 23 The International Energy Agency (IEA) claims that Net-Zero emissions by 2050 requires the timely phasing out oil and gas. 24 The success of the climate change law in phasing out fossil fuels depends on an effective combination of supply-side and demand-side measures. 25 It makes sense to pursue supply-side policies that limit the extraction and supply of fossil fuels as a complement to traditional demandside policies that aim to limit their consumption. While mitigation in fossil fuel consumption must be made by all states, the economic consequences of reduced production will mainly be directed at producing states. 26 enerally, fossil fuel phase out means the immediate cessation of new extraction, infrastructure construction, and the managed reduction of existing production. 27 In fact, it means committing to no new oil and gas exploration or development of new oil and gas fields. 28 By moving away from fossil fuels, states are expected to sacrifice their short-term national development gains for international goals. Therefore, phasing out fossil fuels is necessary to achieve climate goals. 29 hase out policies have been discussed primarily in relation to coal, but the key insights apply equally to oil and gas as well. 30 egarding phasing out fossil fuels, two distinctions should be considered. First, 'unabated' refers to fossil fuels produced and used without interventions that substantially reduce the amount of GHG emitted throughout the life cycle. 31 In contrast, 'abated' refers to the burning of fossil fuels along with the permanent absorption and storage of a portion of the resulting GHGs. 32 However, there is no clarity about what counts as unabated or abated. 33 Second, 'phasing down' refers to a slow transition, while 'phasing out' refers to a rapid and complete elimination. In other words, while phasing out is explicitly about the end goal, phasing down simply indicates reduction. 34 here is disagreement over the difference between them as well.
